And at the end of it, if you see it very closely at the end of it in a very insignificant font, the smallest font possible, they write advertorial. So that it camouflage and you see it as a news item. Advertorial- advertisement plus editorial. So, this is how clipping helps us get new words in the language.  Now acronym, you might have seen abbreviations, right? Where the initial letters are used to represent the whole word. But when these initials or abbreviations are used as a full word independent word. And in cases like, there is a city in near Delhi called Noida… Now, you can find it on Google Map, Noida. Now, that is a place I come from. So, Noida or Greater Noida, so Noida is acronym if you know. And this is being used as an independent, individual word.  And if you go and do the survey, majority of younger people have no idea what is Noida? It is Naveen Okla Industrial Development Authority. But now, these abbreviations N O I D A becomes an acronym because now it is name of a city. A huge city, a well-developed huge city, Noida. So, this is acronym. NATO, we use the word NATO, North Atlantic Treaty Organization. NATO forces, so, NATO. So, NATO is now being used as a single word. So, it contains initials of North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Look at the word called laser, for that matter. Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.  Now, unless you are a physicist, or you are a science student, laser, for a commoner is a word. Scuba, scuba diving you must be doing. What is scuba? Self-Contained Underwater Breathing Apparatus. Now but scuba is being used as a single word. So, this is called acronym when the initials of a larger chunk, abbreviations, constitute a new word. And therefore, they refer to as a single independent word as if they are a word. But essentially, they are abbreviations. Look at ISBN, Inter-State Bus Terminus. But now, it is being used as a single word, that is acronym. This is also a very interesting process of word-formation.  Then blending. Blend means to mix the two. We blend it in such a way that it becomes the word. Like brunch, breakfast and lunch. So, part of breakfast and part of lunch. They are blend together to get a new word, brunch. Words like Cyborg, a blend of cybernetic and organism. So part of cybernetic, part of organism, together they are blended to get, they are blended to get a new word, Cyborg.  Guesstimate, two words, guess and estimate. We blend them in such a way that parts are dropped. And then we get a new word. So, guesstimate, a blend of guess and estimate. These two words are independent words. But out of these two independent words, we get a new word by blending it. Breakfast is an independent word. Lunch is an independent word. But when we add and blend it together, we get brunch, breakfast, and lunch. So, this is blending.  Then, back-formation. Sometimes, if you look at English, new words are created out of an existing word, like resurrection. A single word, there was no word called resurrect. But ion was dropped, and we get a new word. Postpone is a word, but we back-formed another word equivalent, opposite of it, advance. Now we use it, it is in vogue, and we use it. So, what is back-formation? It is a process of creating a new word by removing actual or suppose, a fixation. So possibly we drop… it is like clipping. You drop it, and you create a new word out of it. So, if it is a noun, you get a verb out of it by dropping or clipping of things. So, this is back-formation.  Now, have you ever, ever wondered, have you wondered how we get a word which is not, part of our own language? It comes from other language, but over a period of time, it becomes so frequent, and you know in currency, that it seems like it is our own word. For example, road. It is an English word. School, it is an English word. File, it is an English word. But file for that matter, road, highway for that matter…time, such a, such a frequent, commonly used word. So, we borrow words from other languages depending on the need.  For example, Britishers brought a lot of food items with them to this continent, Indian subcontinent, and you find these food items present in all these languages. Cake, for that matter. Pastry, for that matter. Very rare to find an equivalent of cake in any of the Indian languages, pastry in any of the Indian languages, but we are eating it, and we are using it in such a way that it seems so familiar. Road, school, rail, so these are the words. So, borrowing is a very prolific phenomenon to increase the number of words and vocabulary in a language. And it is across languages, it is never the case that only Indian languages have borrowed from English. English has also borrowed from Indian languages. Particularly let us say, words like loot. A Hindi word, to plunder. Now it's part of Oxford Dictionary. Rita, saree, dharma- the political agitation, lathe, lathe charge. So, it is both ways. Languages come in contact, and we have inflow of new words to the other language and also outflow of words to, towards outside, to different languages. So, it is a very common phenomena. So, borrowing, just taking a word from another language. And look at, look at the English for that matter. English has taken a lot of words from Latin, French, and Greek. You might see all these botanical names of the trees and plants around you. They are all Latin words. And all students of botany, they all know the botanical names of these plants and trees.  So, borrowing is a very…like in Indian language, if you look at, we borrow from each other so much that after a while, it becomes very difficult to find out which word is from where. It is a very prolific phenomenon. In your own native language also, you can know. You can just count and list words which are not originally from your language. But now they are so frequent and in currency, in vogue, that they appear to be your own word. We, we adopt it, and we put it close to our heart, we use it.  If you look at English for that matter, like biology, boxer, ozone, this has been borrowed from German; like jacket, yogurt, kiosk from Turkish; pistol, robot from Czech; dharma, loot, jungle from Hindi. So, this is a very prolific phenomenon that languages borrow from each other. It is not a one-way process. It is a two-way process. Depending on the need, we borrow items. We borrow concepts and all related words with it. You borrow a dress, you borrow a food item, you borrow cultural practice, and you customize it and use it as your own word. This is a very prolific phenomenon in all languages. And English is no exception by the way.  Coinage, see, coin a new term. So, if the word, if the word is lacking, if you have the word is missing, or you find no equivalent of the concept in a language, then we coin a word —Xerox for that matter. Even technology allows us to coin new words. Xerox. Now xerox is the name of the machine company that makes that machine for photocopying. But now Xerox, which is the name of the company, generic, is being used as a verb, and it is used as a word, xerox. Kleenex, the Kodak. These are the names of the company which brought the technology and the idea and the concept, and the concepts are named after them. So, this is another way of doing it.  Then we have compounding, where two words are put together to create a third word to represent a new concept. Like tea and pot. Two separate words, teapot. Lipstick. Lip and stick, lipstick. Lipstick. A new word is a new meaning. By the way, a stick has nothing to do with lip here, lipstick. Breakfast. Fast, a separate word. Break, a separate word. And gives a new word-breakfast. Sunshine babysit, baby oil. Now baby oil, like it is not like mustard oil. When we say mustard oil, oil extracted out of mustard. But baby oil is not oil extracted out of baby, baby oil for baby. So, to be consumed and used for baby, massaging baby.  So, we need to understand that this compounding sometimes change the meaning. So, independent words have a different meaning, but when they are joined together, they give an entirely different meaning. So, mustard oil and baby oil, please, are not the same, we have to keep in mind. Waterproof. Like…bittersweet. So, these are compounding processes and very prolific. And you find in your own language also that how two words just together to get a new word, a third word and how it changes the meaning and how it is used in different contexts to represent different ideas.  Then, inflection. So, there are words, when we use them in sentences, they change the form. These are grammatical functions. So, meaning may not change, but the form changes. Like go, goes, going. And if you put ‘ed’, add to it, went. If you put ‘en’ to it, gone. So, these are called inflections, the process of inflection where use you use a suffix to suit a grammatical requirement, to meet a grammatical requirement in a sentence. So, go and going are two different words with two different purposes. They represent two different things. Like go is in simple verb, but when we say going, it is a progressive form of the simple, same verb, go. If I say went, it is a past form of the same verb. Gone, a past participle form of the same verb go. Or probably baby and babies, are singular, and then we make plural out of it by just adding ‘IES’ in babies.  Sometimes you have superlative, comparative degree in adjectives. So, we say fast, faster, fastest. So, word remains adjective, but we are adding her for comparative degree, for we are adding ‘est’ for superlative degree. So, this process is called inflection.  Then we have a process called derivation. And in derivation, we derive a new word out of already existing word, either by prefixation, so adding something before the word, or by suffixation, adding something after the word. So, let us have some examples like kindness, a word. So, kind is the word and less, a suffix added to it. So, kind is adjective. But the moment we add less, a noun forming suffix, it becomes kindness. So adjective, and if derived noun out of it, adjective is kind, kindness.  You can derive verb like modern, adjective. But the moment I say modernize, I derive modernize from the same word modern, just by adding a suffix to it. And I have a new verb modernize from modern. Capital, capitalize. National, nationalize. So, this is how we derive new words, new categories of words. Then, you can derive adjective out of noun. Recreation, recreational. Nation, national. Temporary.  So, so, you can derive verb out of nouns like glorify. Glory-glorify. Beautify. Beauty-beautify. Simple-simplify. Then you can derive adjective out of verbs, something like drink-a verb. Drinkable. Drinkable-adjective. Likable. Drinkable. You can also derive noun out of verbs, some, deliver, deliverance, delivery. So, you can keep on practicing how we derive nouns out of verbs, how we derive verbs out of nouns, how we derive adjective out of nouns, how we derive adjective out of verb. So, this is a very prolific, productive process where either we use prefix or like, for example, let us say something like power. When we say empower. Large-enlarge. Friend-befriend. So, by just prefixing, we are getting a verb out of it.  And for further understanding of the process, you can just take a look at these books. And you can understand this beautiful process of creating new words in a language and in English, we just talked about. You can think of such processes in your own mother tongue and see what are the processes which are so productive in your mother tongue to create new words. How they are created, modified, derived, how you are giving a new meaning to a word extending the semantic extension we are doing, extending the meaning of the word, the same existing word. Look at technology for that matter, mouse, for that matter. Isn't what we know in IT? We know in computer very well mouse, mouse the function of it. Window, we know window, but it has a different meaning in IT. So, you have the same word with a different extended meaning in different contexts. So, this is a beautiful world of words and keep practicing. We will continue our discussion. For now, this is it. Thank you very much.

title: Required and Optional Elements in English Sentences (Complements and Adjuncts)
text: English - II Professor Rajesh Kumar Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai Required and Optional Elements in English Sentences Welcome to the class. We are looking at sentences. We are specifically going to look at Required and Optional Elements in English Sentences today. Let me give you a footnote on this. Sentences are basic blocks of language. When we talk about accuracy and fluency, we are talking about accurate and grammatical sentences. When we are talking about fluency, we are talking about fluent sentences for our discourse, for our speech, when we speak the language.  Of course, it requires a lot to organize your thought and pick your sentences. And we, we need that, which is organization of thoughts and ability to translate your thoughts into your sentences. We also need to look at appropriateness in sentences. But before all these, what comes is grammatical sentences.  And for us to develop this capability, that is, for us to understand the underlying rules to produce grammatical sentences, is essential. And this comes when we backtrack and look at fundamentals of sentences. All we need to know is to understand what makes a sentence, what are the fundamental components of a sentence. It, it is not a scary. It is very simple. Furthermore, it is mathematical in nature.  Furthermore, it is organized in chunks, and when you understand those parts to construct the whole, or you deconstruct the whole to understand parts, you are going to enjoy the process. And then you are going to see a dramatic impact of you going through these things in your subconscious for producing grammatical sentences.  We know we speak English as non-natives. Maybe some of you speak English as native speakers as well. Meaning, there are some people who started learning language quite early on, and they can be native speakers of Indian English. They can have English as their first language. They can have very good command over English.  Even for them, I suggest, and I request you to backtrack and look at certain aspects of sentences by decomposing them into pieces. And that gives you the confidence. And if you are not the native speaker, you are putting in efforts to learn as an adult that is 15 plus, 15 plus type of learning.  Still, if you need, if you look at these chunks, if you look at how they combine, you observe yourself that you are reaching near-native capacity in terms of grammatical production, in terms of grammatical aspects of your sentences. The sentences that you speak, you see them becoming grammatical-free from errors on their own. So, for that impact, I want you to look at some of these simple aspects. And I want to take you through these aspects to look at these chunks without using any technical jargon so, that you can see how they work.  So, coming back, we are looking at required and optional elements in English sentences. We have heard about English sentences. We know a bit about English sentences. What is this? Are there things that are required in English sentences? Are there things that can be optional in a sentence? What could they be?  I am trying to put them as complements and adjuncts, and you can figure it out from the title itself that complements are sort of required elements in a sentence. And adjuncts are kind of optional elements in a sentence. But we need to know what are complements and what are adjuncts. In under what circumstances one becomes required, and the other becomes optional. What is the role of this, like this optionality? What, what does requirement mean? These are the things that we can answer by looking at these simple aspects of understanding sentences. So let us, let us go ahead and look at these parts.  So, we look at a sentence, and we need to look at its parts. And then when we, when we see the parts, we get a clearer picture. So, when we talk about a sentence, we need to know that there are first, in first attempt we divide them in two parts. One is subject, and second part is predicate. Subject is a, is a separate thing to discuss, but we just want to divide that components into broader parts right now. And we, we will go into the details of those things as we move on.  But, since we are talking about these terms, we must know, know something that connects the two. So, we are, we are talking about two parts subject, predicate. But before we look at predicate, we must know that subject and predicate, they agree with each other. Meaning there is a there is an underlying-hidden bond between the two.  And that bond is called agreement, which is yet another thing, and we will discuss that. When we go and look at predicates, we see it has several kinds of components, but the most important part is a verb. The reason why we call it most important part is because all of, all other components within predicate are, in one way or the other, connected with this verb. Their existence is contingent upon this verb. Therefore, this is the most important component.  And this is the reason why many a time, when people say predicate, they mean verbs. But literally speaking, verbs are one single unit and predicate, the term predicate is used for everything that is associated with verb in that sentence. So, the verbs can be of two types- transitives and intransitives. And given these two types of verbs, this is part of the nature of verb. We, the verbs, decide whether they have objects or not.  So sometimes they have one object when they are transitive verbs. Sometimes, some transitive verbs have two objects, which are called ditransitive verbs. And some verbs have no objects. They are called intransitive verbs. So, see how objects and their existence is contingent upon the nature of verb. So, that is, that way, they are part of the verb. And, they are so closely tied with each other, that they are called, they are, they are part of one phrase, which is known as verb phrase. And in that way, objects become complements of the verb.  And then we have adjuncts or adverbs, which modify or describe the verb, but are not contingent upon the verb. That is, their existence is not contingent upon the verb. The nature of verb, that is transitive or intransitive nature of verb, does not dictate the presence or absence of adverbs. In that sense, they are not directly connected. But in a very indirect way, they are still associated with verbs. So, when objects become complements, adjuncts become... adverbs become adjuncts, and they remain adjuncts. So that is the distinction between complement and adjuncts. So, objects are complements, and adverbs are adjuncts. We need to see how they work for a sentence.  So, what we need to notice about a sentence, and we need to keep in mind about a sentence, as we develop our understanding of a sentence, is all sentences are going to have subjects and predicates. These are required elements of a sentence, required components of a sentence. We are only talking about English in this class. So, we can say all English sentences will have subject and predicates.  But just as a side note, I must let you know this is the rule for all sentences of all the languages of the world. They will have these two parts. The order of words in the English sentence is this way. You have subjects. So these are the two parts. Subjects part one, predicate part two. But within the predicate also you are going to have verbs preceding the objects, or we can say objects follow the verb.  In, in our languages, like Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali, Assamese, Marathi, Hindi, we have objects preceding the verb. Therefore, our languages are called verb final languages and English happens to be verb medial language. This is one major structural difference between our languages and English. There are many, but one major structural difference lies in the order of words within a predicate.  So, what we need to know, so these are the two things that we need to know —one about subject and predicate, two about order of elements within the predicate. And then finally, as I mentioned, subjects on one side, and verbs, within a predicate, these two things perform some sort of agreement between each other in all English sentences.  And that is how they do not remain two separate entities. That is how they get connected with one another. If we, if we do not say a thing about this connection, then it seems like we are talking about two separate disjoint entity of a sentence. So, please understand, subjects and predicates are two parts of a sentence, but they are not completely disjoint entity. They are connected. They are harmonized with agreement between the two.  So, we will get back to agreement. But moving ahead, to talk about complements and adjuncts and how they work, here is yet another thing that we need to know. So, again, let us look at an example of this thing. John loves Mary. This is a subject, and this is a this whole thing is predicate.  This part in red indicates agreement. This indicates a singular number and third person for the purpose of agreement, which is contingent upon singular and third person of the subject. So, just a moment ago, I was talking about agreement with you. I have just underlined this marker of agreement, which is, which connects the two. It, it works in multiple ways. It is not the same all the time.  So, in this sentence, it surfaces as this one. In some sentences, they do not surface. In some sentences, they surface in different ways. That, that we will discuss separately, but these are the two parts of the sentence predicate. Now, look at the predicate. This is the verb, love, which is a transitive verb, and it requires an object. And this one, Mary, is the object of this transitive verb, love.  Thus, this becomes a verb phrase. So, all three components of the sentence are required components. So, Mary is a complement in this sentence, that is, complement of the verb. John likes pizza with his friends. Look at this sentence. This is slightly longer. So, this complement Mary becomes the required element of this sentence.  Look at the next sentence. John likes pizza. Again, this is an agreement marker. Pizza is the complement of this verb. Because it is an object of this verb, it is part of the verb phrase. But with his friends, is an additional piece of information. It is a prepositional phrase, where, with is a preposition. And his friends, again, is a nominal element.  So, this is a this is a prepositional phrase, which provides additional information. Now, we need to figure out this provides additional information about what? I want you to wait for a moment here and think about this. I have been talking about the required elements and additional element.  Pizza is the required element of the sentence because it is required by the verb. It is the object of the verb. Hence, it is a complement of the verb. Now, with his friends, is, is an additional element. It is not required. But therefore, it is an adjunct, not a compliment. But the question is, it is an adjunct of what? John likes pizza with his friends. So, is it about likes, or is it about pizza? That is all we need to decide.  So, John likes with his friends, John likes pizza with his friends. So, is this element with his friends, giving us some information about pizza, or about liking. I leave it here and come back to this to give you a couple of minutes for you to think about this problem. Now, look at it —John and Mary, here, like pizza in the evening.  Think about it. This is a plural subject. So here, the plurality is marked with nothing. Zero means nothing. So, no marker, in an overt fashion appears on the verb to mark plurality, when we have a plural verb. So, no plurality, no person, nothing. And as it is gender surfaces in the context of agreement, in a very limited way, in English.  So, there are three parts that are components of agreement-number, person and gender. Gender surfaces in a very limited way. Once again, we will leave that aside. Let us get back to the main point. John and Mary like pizza. Here is the subject, here is the verb and here you have object of the verb, which is a compliment. This much is, these are required elements of a sentence. In the evening, is certainly, an additional piece of information. It is about time. It gives us time information.  But think about it. What does this give information about? Is it about pizza, again, or liking? Again, I want you to think about this. When you compare these two sentences, the question that I am asking you to figure out from your understanding and your exercise of looking at the elements of these things, and if you follow my discussions, it should be much easier for you to look at it. And I am asking you, I am taking you forward leading your thought into this direction for you to see that.  So, I come back to that part in a moment. If you need, you can pause here. You can think about it because the kinds of things that we are going to discuss forward will help us make this decision. But let me assure you, you can make this decision right here as well. And if you, if you have figured it out by now, then you know a major and subtle aspect of English sentence. And this is going to fill you with confidence. And this will have impact on your understanding of grammaticality of a sentence. Let us move ahead.  There are some of, some sentences are of this type. Come here. Is this not a...this is a full sentence. Is this not a sentence? It is a sentence. It is a full sentence. These types of sentences are called imperative sentences, which are about some sort of, some sort of request. So, when we say tell somebody come here, what we mean is, you come here. So in all imperative sentences, you become the subject of the sentence. It is a very typical question, question that we ask all the time... do imperative sentences have subjects or not? People also give us these examples. When we say all English sentences must have subject, they come up with this, when we say, come here, we do not have a subject in this sentence. At this point, you could have figured out by now that this sentence has a subject. It is just that when we speak, we do not overtly speak that subject. The reason is very simple.  You can, you can look at imperative sentences, all imperative sentences of English, all imperative sentences of all the languages of the world. Human mind kind of figures it out that when the subject is always only one element, you, that is second-person pronoun, then why to articulate it? This is called, this is an evidence of language, being a sophisticated product of human mind that when it is obvious, it must not be articulated. This is also known as principle of economy and operating that principle in production of language, that we do not, we do not articulate the subject, but we know it is there. So basically, absence of something is also registering its presence. So, we know, that there is a subject in this sentence. But it is absent because it is predictable. Moving ahead. So, when we say come here, it comes as an intransitive, intransitive verb. It does not need an object.  So, here is indicative of the, the location, that this is an adverb, an adjective in the sentence. When we say sit down, we have no adjunct. Since it is an intransitive verb, it does not need an object. And it is, it is a it is a complete thing by itself, and there is no adjunct in this. Now, next, look at this. Drink a glass of water before food sounds like medical advice from a doctor. But, when we try to understand this sentence, when we say drink, it is a transitive verb.  And a glass of water as a noun phrase is the object of this transitive verb. And this object is, is the complement of this verb phrase. This much is required, required because the absence of it is again leaving the sentence incomplete. But in this case of drink, I am sure you would know that you must have heard this thing, but I am going to underline this nonetheless. Drink is one special case, special verb in English or for that matter in any language. When we do not specify an object, that is when the complement of this verb remains absent, then it means alcohol. So, when we can say, do not drink, that means do not drink alcohol. So, absence of this is, this is the peculiar thing about this verb. That without specifying the object, it means alcohol. So, you must have read, you must have seen these things do not drink. It is written at a lot of places, do not drink and drive. So, when we say do not drink, we do not specify do not drink what.  So, without specifying the answer what, means alcohol. If you want to, to mean anything else, that is, you want to say do not drink something in particular, then you must specify that. Nonetheless, it is, it has an object in this sentence, and this completes it. Before the bed is an adjunct. This is not required element by the verb. But when it is present, it gives us information about what? A glass of water or drinking? Again, you need to think about it, and we come back to that, we will resolve it.  So, now we can see a complement is an essential, structurally indispensable part of a sentence clause or a phrase. It is an indispensable part, remember that. It is, we cannot remove it from a sentence. Because when we remove it makes the sentence incomplete, it makes the sentence ungrammatical. These are the terms that we need to remember. So, how does it make a sentence incomplete? Look at these following examples. AJU needs for his exam. How does this sentence sound to you? AJU needs for his exam. You can, you can always ask, if, if it sounds incomplete to you needs what, and then we say whatever he needs for the exam is missing from this sentence.  What we mean in simple words is, it is missing an object. That is, object of the verb need. So, it could be a pen, it could be a notebook, or it can be something whatever fills in that gap. AJU needs that. We can, we can leave this part aside and then it is not ungrammatical. If, if we say AJU needs a pen.  For his exam, it is not essential to complete the sentence. There is nothing missing in the sentence. However, if we say that as well, AJU needs a pen for his exam, then for his exam becomes an additional piece of information about something in within that predicate. And therefore, this is an adverb or adjunct.  But this is an object, and this verb is missing its complement. Same way, RAM eats after dinner. Eats what after dinner? So, we can say, takes medicines, eats an apple, or eats something after dinner... sweets... so that something is missing from this sentence. So, without completing that grid, the sentence is incomplete. And that is what I am trying to show you. And hence, it becomes ungrammatical as well. Therefore, an object, a complement is structurally indispensable.  It must be present in this structure, unlike adjuncts. Seems reads in the morning. She reads, Seems reads in the morning. That is fine, but she reads what? Maybe she reads a newspaper in the morning. Maybe she reads a novel in the morning. Maybe she reads a story in the morning. So that answer to what is still missing from here. Without that, this is an incomplete sentence. So, hope you get a picture of what is a complement.  Same way, we say adjuncts, an adjunct is an optional entity. Which here we can say, it is structurally dispensable element of a sentence, a clause or a phrase. And if we remove it, it does not, does not structurally affect the formation of a sentence. That is, so what does this tell you? Adjuncts are not structurally required in the sense that, an absence of adjuncts does not structurally make a sentence ungrammatical.  So, we need to know the distinction between these two to understand what is, what makes the sentences structurally grammatical, complete, or incomplete. What are the elements that are, okay, we speak these things, we need these things, but they are not structurally important? So, to get an idea of the required things, to complete the structure of a sentence in English, this discussion is important. And it gives you a different kind of confidence for yourself.  So, look at the examples of the sentences of this part. AJU helped RAM in the morning. Perfect. AJU is the subject, helped is the verb, RAM is the object of this verb help in the morning. So, this is an adjunct, in the morning. This is giving information about what? What did... in the morning is time, indicating time? So, it is easy for us to figure out that it is talking about help in the morning.  So, it is modifying the verb. AJU, when you have this missing, helped in the morning after breakfast...you have two adverbs here. Both are giving you time. But the object is missing from here. So, when an object is missing, that is when complement is missing, then this sentence becomes ungrammatical. Whereas, when you have another adjunct missing, or the whole adjunct missing, the sentence is not ungrammatical. This is an important part that we need to remember.  So, before we move forward in this discussion, I want you, I want to go back and look at it. AJU drinks a glass of water before bed. Before bed is an adverb, adjunct of this water. What does h e do? text: English 2 Ms. Parthia Sathyanathan Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology Madras Chennai Punctuations - Pauses – I Hello, all, welcome. Today, we will talk about punctuations. What in punctuations? We will look at pauses.  So, there are three marks that fall under this category. That is the comma, semicolon, and the colon. Now, before we get to these, let me talk to you about pause. What is a pause? Well, with these three marks, the pause tells you that the reader should stop briefly and then continue reading. So when you see a comma or a semicolon or a colon, you need to briefly stop and then continue reading.  Let us start with comma. So let me make this clear. It is not pronounced as comma or comma, but comma. So the comma has four main uses. The first is to separate items from the list. I have given an example here. I have to buy cereals, pulses, milk, and eggs from the supermarket. So here, you see that there are four items given in the sentence. That is, cereals, pulses, milk, and eggs. These items are actually separated by comma.  Now in schools, your teachers would have taught you that you should not put a comma before and. That is, at this place. But that is not really true. You may or may not use a comma before and. However, if there are only two items, then you do not put a comma. What I mean to say is, in case, in the second sentence, which is I have to buy milk and sugar from the supermarket. You will not put a comma, or you should not put a comma after milk. That is wrong. So, the rule is put comma after every list, except the last. I hope that is clear to you.  Now, the second use of comma is to separate words that are not part of the sentence. Now, what do you mean by words that are not part of a sentence? By that, I mean to talk about the main sentence. So, let me give you an example. The example sentence is, unfortunately, I did not attend the class. In this sentence, the main sentence is, I did not attend the class, and unfortunately is actually the speaker’s opinion. That is called the sentence adverb.  So, in this case, the sentence adverb unfortunately, is separated from the main sentence using a comma. So, whenever you see a sentence adverb, separated with a comma, what are the other sentence adverbs that we have? We could use fortunately, frankly, hopefully, sadly, luckily... the list is long.  Now, when it comes to forms of address, like when you use name or when you use the expression Sir or Ma’am, you need to separate that from the sentence using a comma. Two examples are given here. 'Riga, can you please hold this bucket for a second?' This is a question, and in this question, the form of address that is the name Riga is separated by a comma. Now the second sentence is. 'Sir, please come inside.' So again, the form of address Sir, the expression Sir, is separated by a comma.  The next point or the next category is formal letters and emails. So, when it comes to salutations or greetings in formal letters or emails, such as what, Dear Sir, Dear Ma’am, Dear Sir and Ma’am or when you address by the name Dear Riga, you use comma. But you would also have seen colon. So, now the question is, should I use comma, or should I use colon? Well, the answer is, it depends on the context. So, if you are writing to an American company, then you need to use the American way, which is a colon. So, after the salutation or greeting, you use a colon there. But in British English, that is, the standard English, we need to put a comma after the salutation or greeting. Similarly, in the closing expressions, you need to put a comma at the end. That is, yours faithfully comma, yours sincerely comma. And this is true for both American and British English.  The next function of comma is to separate linking words. What are linking words? Words like however, therefore, for example, in fact, etc., are linking words. Let me explain that by giving you some example sentences. So, let us look at the sentence, 'She has not got many friends. However, everyone likes her.' So, here the linking word, however comes at the beginning of the sentence. Therefore, you separate this linking word with a comma.  Another example is, 'My dog knows many tricks. In fact, he can bark on command.' So there again, the linking word, in fact, comes in the beginning of the sentence, and therefore, we separate it with a comma. Let us look at the second sentence, 'She has not got many friends. Everyone, however, likes her.' In this case, the linking word, however, comes in between the sentence.  So, in that case, you need to separate this linking word with two commas, that is, at its beginning and at its end. So, this is how you write it. 'She has not got many friends.  Everyone, however, everyone likes her.' Similarly, look at the sentence, 'My dog knows many tricks. He can, in fact, bark on command.'  Now, what if the linking word comes at the end of the sentence? 'She has not got many friends. Everyone likes her, however.' In that case, you will separate this however with a comma, and because it comes at the end of the sentence, full stop automatically takes over the comma. So, with the full stop, the sentence ends. The other example sentence is, 'My dog knows many tricks. He can bark on my command, in fact.'  Did I make that clear? I hope so.  Now, we are coming to the fourth use of commas, that is, to separate clause. This is slightly tricky. I want you to pay closer attention to this, and if you have got any doubts with that, please put up your queries in the discussion forum. So, before I get to talk about commas and clauses, I need to talk to you about clause.  So, there are two types of clause, the independent clause, which is a complete sentence and then the dependent clause, which is not the complete sentence. It needs an independent clause to complete and form a proper sentence. So, I have given examples here. I attended music class last month. So, that is an independent clause because it is complete by itself. It does not require another sentence to make it meaningful or proper. So, that is independent clause.  Now, 'When Lena gets home from work', so you may ask what? Lena gets home from work, and so what? So, which means the sentence is not complete. So, therefore this is called a dependent clause. It needs something else to complete itself. So, if you add another independent clause like 'she practices violin for an hour' to the dependent clause, that is, 'when Lena gets home from work,' it becomes a complete proper sentence. 'When Lena gets home from work, she practices violin for an hour.' So, that becomes a main sentence.  Now, there are many different ways of forming a sentence. It could be by bringing together two independent clauses. It could be by bringing together a dependent clause first and then an independent clause. You could form a sentence by putting an independent clause first and then a dependent clause or what is known as a non-essential clause.  So, there are different rules of using comma with the different variants. So, let us discuss that. So, the first one is when two independent clauses comes together. So, let us see what are two independent clauses here. I have given an example, 'he kicked the ball'. The other independent clause is, 'they won the match.' So, when you bring together two independent clauses, you need to put a comma after the first. So, you need to write, 'He kicked the ball, they won the match.' But is that all enough? No. When you bring together two independent clauses, and you put a comma after the first, you also need to connect these two clauses with coordinating conjunctions. What are coordinating conjunctions? Words like and, or, but, so, etc. So you could say, 'He kicked the ball, and they won the match.' Or you could also say, 'He kicked the ball, so they won the match.' Now, when you miss the 'and' that is a coordinating conjunction after the comma, then that kind of error is called the comma splice. So, this is a very common error that people commit. Even fluent users of language commit this mistake while writing. They skip, or they do not use the coordinating conjunction that must and definitely follow the comma when you bring together two independent clauses. So, I hope I made that clear.  Now, the next variant is when you have a dependent clause with an independent clause to form the main sentence. For example, the example sentence I have given you here is, 'If you get good grades, I will take you to London.' So here, the parent is driving his kid, saying, if you get good grades, I will take you to London.  So, in this case, if you get good grades is what? It is a dependent clause because it does not exist by, or it does not sound meaningful by itself. If you get good grades, so yes, what? So, what? It is added to an independent clause, which is I will take you to London. So, when you bring together a dependent clause and an independent clause, you need to put a comma after the dependent clause, that is, the first clause.  But you do not put 'and' like how we used it in the previous example because there we were bringing together two independent clauses. So here, since it is a dependent clause and an independent clause, we are not going to put an 'and'. That would be wrong. So, it would not make sense if you say, 'If you get good grades, and I will take you to London.' Nor will it make sense if you say, 'If you get good grades and I will take you to London', without a comma there. So, both those sentences are wrong. What is right is, 'If you get good grades, I will take you to London.'  Now the next variant is you have an independent clause at the beginning, followed by a dependent clause. 'He was so happy when he won the match!' So, 'When he won the match' is the dependent clause that follows the independent clause 'he was so happy'. So, in this case, you should not separate the independent clause from the dependent clause with a comma. Here, strictly, no comma. So, you should not be writing, 'He was so happy, when he won the match! That is wrong. Putting a comma here is wrong.  So, the next example introduces us to a type of dependent clause called the relative or the adjectival clause. It is also called an adjectival clause because it gives information about the noun. So, a relative clause is introduced by a relative pronoun. And what are relative pronouns? Who, which, whom, that, these are all relative pronouns or a related adverb like when, where, why.  So in this sentence, 'That man is the criminal who shot his neighbor last month,' the relative clause is 'who shot his neighbor last month.' Why? Because it gives us the information about the noun, which is 'criminal'. That is, it tells us who the criminal is. Now, what happens when we remove that clause? That man was what criminal you could ask if we remove that clause.  Now, if I remove the clause 'who shot the neighbor last month,' the sentence would be, 'that man is the criminal.' 'That man is the criminal.' 'What criminal?' is the question that follows after the sentence. If someone hears the sentence, 'that man is the criminal,' 'That man is the criminal.' Criminal for what?  So, to make that complete, you need to say, 'That man is the criminal who shot his neighbor last month.' Therefore, when we remove the clause, it becomes meaningless or incomplete. So, this relative clause cannot be removed from the sentence and therefore, it is called the essential clause. So the rule is, we do not use comma for essential clause. What is the rule? The rule is we do not use comma for essential clause.  Now, the next example is 'People love to celebrate New Year’s Eve, which is the last day of the year.' The clause 'which is the last day of the year' can be removed because, without that clause, the sentence 'People love to celebrate New Year’s Eve' makes perfect sense. The meaning is still clear. Therefore, it is called a non-essential clause. We separate non-essential clause with a comma. So, we do not separate essential clause with a comma, but we separate non-essential clause with a comma.  Now, let us move to the next example. 'My cousin Nisha, whom you met at the party is heading to US tomorrow.' Here, the relative clause 'whom you met at the party' is in the middle of the sentence. It gives information about Nisha, my cousin Nisha, whom you met at the party is heading to US tomorrow. So, this particular clause is giving information about Nisha.  So let me ask you, is this an essential or non-essential clause? Well, it is a non-essential clause, because you can remove that, and still, the sentence would make perfect sense. My cousin Nisha is heading to US tomorrow. It sounds perfect. It sounds meaningful. Therefore, this is non-essential clause. So, we separate it from the rest of the sentence using comma. But here, we used two commas this time, because the relative clause is in the middle of the sentence.  So, these are all the rules for punctuating the clause correctly. So here, we separate this clause from the rest of the sentence using two commas, which is at its beginning and at its end.  Now, the next use of comma is to use it before quotation. An example is given here. The quotation is, 'It is a warm day.' The sentence is, 'He said, "It is a warm day."' So, you put the quotation in quotes, and you separate it from the rest of the sentence using a comma. So, in this case, you need to put a comma after he said. So, that is all with punctuating clauses correctly.  Now, I have given you a few questions for practice. Add comma whenever necessary. The first one is, 'They played chess until it was time to go home.' The second one is, 'Since there was no school that day the children played in the snow.' The third sentence is, 'We thought she was nice because she smiled a lot.' Fourth sentence is, 'While the class took a test the teacher graded papers' and the fifth sentence is, 'She said “He is a nice person.”' Pause the video for some time. Solve these questions, and then, let us discuss the answers.  The answers are shown here. 'She said, He is a nice person.' It is a quotation. So, it needs to be separated from the quote. The sentence needs to be separated from the quote. So we are putting a comma before the quote. The next one is, 'While the class took a test the teacher graded the papers.' So this is what, this is a dependent clause, and the teacher graded the paper is an independent clause. So, when dependent plus independent clause comes, you need to separate them with a comma.  'We thought she was nice because she smiled a lot.' Now, 'we thought she was nice.' This is what independent clause and 'because she smiled a lot' is dependent clause. So, when independent plus dependent clause comes together, then you do not use comma. The second example is, 'Since there was no school that day the children played in the snow.'  So what is this, 'Since there was no school that day'? It does not make sense when it stands alone. So, it means it is a dependent clause plus, what does this mean? 'The children played in the snow,' it can stand independently. Therefore, it is dependent plus independent clause. Therefore, it needs to be separated by a comma. And what is the first example? 'They played chess until it was time to go home.'  So, this is 'They played chess' is independent and 'until it was time to go home,' followed by dependent. So here again, no comma. So, I hope it was clear to all of you. So, with this, we come to the end of the session. I will meet you with a different topic on a different day. Until then, stay safe. Take care, bye.

title: Writing
text: English – II Ms Parthia Sathyanathan Department of Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Resume Hello all, welcome to this module. Today, we will discuss writing resumes. So, when I talk about resumes, the first thing that students ask is, what is the difference between a resume and CV. CV stands for curriculum vitae, and CV is the long history of all that you have done, which is the work history, the longer version, whereas the shorter version of your curriculum vitae is what we call the resume.  Resume generally runs for one to two page. At max, you should have two pages and not more than that. So, I have taken a few snippets of my resume in order to discuss a few points that I think is important when we talk about resume writing.  Now start your resume with your full name and then the area of residence. So, I stay in Chennai; therefore I write Chennai there, along with your contact information, first the phone number and then the Gmail ID or your email ID. Then comes a very important point, which are you should always write an overview of your resume. Why this? Because your boss or the interviewer or the manager of the company will not have time to read or go through your entire CV or your resume. So, it is important that you give a brief overview with all the important points that you think their attention should go.  So, it is important that you come up with a precise overview, which has all the important points that you think your manager should go through. So, here let us read out the overview that I have in my CV, that I have in my resume. I have graduated from IIT Madras with an integrated Masters in English Studies from the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences in 2015. So, IIT Madras, in bold your institution, the institution from where you have graduated is very important, and what is, what else is important is the year in which you have graduated. So, these two I am highlighting in bold. Now the second line, why have I marked that in yellow? It is because you should not include such lines in your CV. I am a result-oriented and performance-driven development professional with more than five years of experience, no. Your qualities, it is for the manager to find out, it is for the CV to speak the work that you have done so far will talk about your qualities, so you should not speak for yourself, you should not speak about your qualities.  So, I have seen the lot of students writing, I am a very hardworking professional, which is not required. And similarly, if you look at the sentence I have, I am a result-oriented and performance-driven development professional with more than five years of experience, be precise. Do you have 5.5 years of experience? Write 5.5 years of experience, do you have 8 years of experience? Write 8 years of experience, even 20 years is more than 5 years of experience. So be very precise. Then in my career, I have led the design and implementation of various interventions to improve the quality of education. So, here I have broadly written what my area of work is, which is education. My expertise lies in academic and action research, teaching, design and implementation of projects and leading large-scale multilateral projects with the government and non-government organizations. Again, very important.  Please do not confuse your passion with that of expertise. Lot of students I have seen they have written that teaching is their area of expertise. And when I ask them what have you thought? They say, no, I have not thought anything, but I know that I am a good teacher, or I am skilled at teaching, no. Your area of expertise, you can mention all that only if you have done that only if you have experience in those areas.  Similarly, it is also important for you to talk about the people whom you have associated yourself with for the work that you have done, here. So, I have written I am proficient and working with a diverse range of stakeholders, including bureaucrats, knowledge partners, government organizations, school principals, teachers and students. I work in educational research and practice and the primary areas of interest include linguistics, linguistic education, multilingualism, multiculturalism, social inclusion and policy and governance.  So, I had included this line at a time when I was looking for some research positions as well. So, this overview is a good blend of academic and non-academic work. So, someone who goes through it, kinds of read, or it is quite explicit from the overview that I have done both academic and non-academic work. So, your target should be that if you are perfect at managerial work, highlight those parts. And if you are looking for a managerial position, highlight those parts in particular. If you are looking for academic position then highlight those parts of your work.  The next is publications. Maybe not everybody is interested in publishing, but I would say that if you have publications, it is definitely a brownie point. Maybe you are not inclined towards academics in which case you can write some editorials for some well-known newspapers or some well-known magazines; they are all brownie points, I must tell you. This definitely speaks a lot about your passion, your talent then your interest in public or social issues.  Next comes research experience. All of you can definitely add your thesis, bachelor's thesis, which will be close to what six months to one year. As a part of your research experience, if you have more research experience to add it up. The thing that you need to note here is, use different verbs to talk about your work.  Here I have used worked, conducted, rated, tested. Do not keep using just one verb such as worked. I have seen a lot of kids write worked for this thing, I worked in this thing, I worked for that. Rather than use vivid or different verbs to describe your work or the nature of work you have done.  Next comes Awards and Scholarships. Write everything that comes to your mind. Every single award and scholarship that you have got. Again, you can highlight important points that you think the jury or the manager should look at.  Next comes Professional Experience. The internships that you have done can also be included in the professional experience. So, all that you have, so far, I am pretty sure you would have done a couple of internships or maybe worked before taking up this course. You can add all that as a part of your professional experience.  Then comes the Education and Skills. In the column for education, you write the program, then the institution and the percentage and CGPA and then the year of completion. Similarly, it is very important for you to write about skills because that speaks a lot about you, what your passion is, what you have done so far in life.  So, as a part of skills, you can write your technical skills, language skills and then your hobbies. Language skills, English, Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam Sanskrit and French, Microsoft Access and Adobe Photoshop. Trained Bharatanatyam dancer for four years, skilled in painting and crafting.  And finally, you can write about the position of responsibility, particularly the one that you have had in your college. So, you could say your, I was a curriculum coordinator back then, I was also a part of the NSS National Service Scheme as a volunteer, so all that can be written as positions of responsibility. So that was a short tutorial on resume writing. I hope you liked the session. I will meet you with a different topic on a different day. Until then stay safe. Take care. Bye.

title: Interview Skill - 1
text: English II Professor Om Prakash Guest Faculty, Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Chennai Welcome to class. We are going to talk about some very important issues in the process of interview and placement. So, your entire effort for years in preparing and studying getting a degree culminates into a job interview. You go for a job, and you are subjected to structured interview.  So, today we will talk about what skills are required to get placed after interviews, or what skills are required to impress a panel of selectors who interview you. Let me tell you communication is an art, so there is no shortcut and I cannot suggest you rule number 1, 2, 3, 4 which will help you in interviews. But there are certain things we need to pay attention to.  At the same time, we need to understand that interviews that we face during job selection, job interviews during selections are all impressionistic. So, you need to create a lasting impression to be registered in the clutter. Because mind you when you go for an interview, you have a lot of competitions and a lot of people are there your competitors, your rivals are there, your peers are there. And more or less broadly, they contain similar level of knowledge and everyone answers those questions in the interview fairly similar way.  But what makes the difference? Why certain answers are registered, certain candidates are registered, certain candidates impress the panel and get a place. So, there is no golden rule for that, I repeat. But we need to evolve as an effective communicator. We need to work on our linguistic skills. We need to work on our communicative skills. Furthermore, we need to work on our overall impression and image apart from the technical degree that you have, apart from the grades and distinctions you have. So, let us talk about interview skills, what skills are required and what skills we need to focus on.  Now, there are certain challenges that we face before going for a job interview. Anxiety, of course is the biggest thing. An anxiety of all kinds, imagined fears, anxieties, apprehensions. This anxiety leads to nervousness. So, you, if you are very anxious before the interview, you, when you enter the room, you will feel nervous. You become overcautious, that I should not make a mistake. The fear of mistake makes you overcautious and leads you to hypercorrection.  And part of this problem is lack of preparation for the interview at both the levels. A t personal levels as a person, though there is a problem in your grooming; at the level of awareness about the organization you are going to be interviewed by and also the technical knowledge which is required for the job profile; are you prepared for that or not? So, preparation of all kinds when we lack, we lack confidence.  When we lack the control over content, it is a challenge to us, it is problematic. And then because of all these trailing problems, connected problems, our communication strategy, our interactive skills, lack of interactive skills lead to all kinds of anxiety and improper body language. Your confidence is shaken, and your body language reflects that, that lack of confidence, nervousness. Your body language reflects that, your eye contact for that matter, your tone for that matter. Paralinguistic items like tone, pitch, rhythm, your voice become shaky, your body language does, your reflexes become inappropriate. And because you do not have control on the content of the interview, you resort to lots of distractions. So, you have been asked something else, your answer is something else, you are not straightforward, you are not hitting the bulls eye.  So, these are the problems that we all have and believe me it can happen at any stage. There is not only on freshers, problem on freshers, but the established people in their field if they are not prepared, they will face these challenges, and they have to overcome these challenges. So, it is not unusual; this is quite normal and natural. But these challenges are not as big that you cannot surmount and control them.  You can control them; you can bring them in your control, you can be confident, you can be prepared, you can be confident, you can show control over the content, you can be pleasing and register yourself in the memory of those panel members who are there for you to select.  Now, there are three stages of an interview. Few things which are required before the interview happens; we call it pre-interview preparations. Then there are certain things we have to keep in mind and which is the while-interview situation and finally, the third stage is post-interview where we do a lot of follow-up activities. So, we will talk about all these three stages of interview; pre-interview, while-interview and post-interview by and by one after the other.  So, we will talk about pre-interview first. So, there are certain things we have to keep in mind while preparing for an interview. First and foremost, you have to mentally oriented towards the interview. If you look at the format of the interview, oral interview I mean, these days because of pandemic we have telephonic interviews which makes our life easy but also poses another set of challenges. We will not talk about that. Let us image a normal formal oral interviews. So, as a fresher, you do not possess an experience of job, and you are a fresher going for an interview for the first time. We all believe that if I speak too much, there are certain myths associated with an interview that if he speaks fluently, if he speaks at high range, if the delivery of per minute words are high, if I speak in louder voice, if I speak with smile on the face, so all kinds of myths are there.  First and foremost, relax, you do not have to act like some other person, be your usual self. This is the first thing. Do not panic. Do not overdo anything, you have to be just what you are. You have to believe in what you are. First and foremost, you have to believe in yourself that generates a lot of confidence. Be what you are; you need not try and be someone else.  You might have seen people in the formal domain do a lot of acting. Acting is not advisable for an interview. You have to be relaxed, composed, voiced and confident. And that comes from the belief in your efficacy. The efficacy the belief that you can do it. We do not have to act like another person, be what you are. But you need to prepare beforehand certain things like research about the organization which is going to interview you, you have applied for, and you are going to be interviewed.  Because familiarity with the organization will help you imagine and practice some predictable questions. Understanding of the organization, information about the organization also prepares you better to respond effectively. It also orients you towards the nature and culture of the organization. You can imagine the people from the organization, what kind of people you are going to have, going to find, the functions. As an icebreaker in the first phase of the interview, sometimes interviewers have this idea of talking in general, talking about you and talking about your knowledge of the organization. So, you have to do a thorough research about the organization you have applied and going to be interviewed by. Then, you have to imagine certain predictable questions. See, always remember, though interview does not follow any strict structure, but by and large all such interviews are structured conventionally.  And if you look at the stages inside, during that interview inside the room, you find a set of questions, few questions which work as icebreaker. So, they ask you general questions about tell me about yourself. This is very predictable question. Introduce yourself, it is a very predictable question. Explain yourself as a person, so the wordings can be anything, but you have to talk about yourself, you have to talk your academic background, sometimes family background.  So, these are the standard questions, and you do not need any extra preparation for that. Only thing is that you need to prioritize and sequence the information you are going to give for these questions. So, when you are asked for your academic background, what are the things that you are going to highlight, what are the things that you are going to talk about and you are free. So, you have to focus on the positive aspects of your academic background, and also you have to prompt them to ask diverse questions on your background.  So, you have to give them information, interesting information. So, you have to do the packaging. So, you have to package yourself as a product and market yourself. So, you might have seen this marketing skills where we talk about the quality of the product, value of the product. So, you as a person and your academic background, your family background, do the packaging well. You have to prepare for certain predictable answers.  Then they may talk about your hobbies, predictable question, very universal predictable question. If you have some achievements in your career, in your academic background, then talk about it, highlight that. So, this is what I mean by packaging. You have to package yourself in such a way that more interesting things and salient achievements of your career must be highlighted and recorded. That prompts them to ask more about it. So, you have to just trigger certain ideas, and they will ask more questions about it. So, do the packaging well.  Then they move to the core academic questions, technical round. So, the second stage after the ice breaking, they move to technical round where they ask about your knowledge, your awareness, you're training, your exposure, some more training if you have done. So, all these questions. So, they check, and they test they evaluate your technical understanding of the profile for the job you are doing.  Then they, the third stage of the interview moves into testing, evaluating or examining your adaptability. So, you as a person how flexible you are. Questions like you applied for the position in Chennai or in Delhi, what if we post you at Pune or some other location? It is just to check whether you are open to such unimagined, unexpected challenger or not. They test you as a team worker, so they will frame questions in such a way that reflects you as a team worker.  So, you have to prove that you are going to be an asset to the organization if you are hired. Because of your professional commitment, because of your handwork, because of your curiosity and to learn new things, because you are not scared of challenges, and you are ready to take challenges. So, these skills are tested in the third place when your technical thing is over, they are satisfied, they will move to the third part of the interview.  And the fourth part is conclusion, wrapping up, closing the interview. So, they will ask questions about your preferences of the profile, types of job you are expecting, the place you want to be placed, maybe the salary component will be discussed. So, broadly you can guess there are certain questions very predictable. But the problem is that even if we can guess certain questions, we do not do practice.  So, what you have to do? You have to anticipate, imagine and note down some predictable, generic universal questions in your field of expertise, you as a professional and you as a person in your personal round and finally your expectations from this job. So, your salary, your position, you're posting, so all these things. This is the broad content of an oral interview for a job, and we all know it, but we do not prepare. So, preparation is very important before the interview.  Be in control means once you are prepared and once you have packaged yourself, you have revised your answers of those imagined predictable questions, you feel confident. Make notes and also evaluate your own answers that you are preparing. You have to develop control over the content and always remember, nobody is interested to ask you theories. The questions that they frame in job interviews are more of application oriented.  So, the theories that you have learned, the concepts that you have learned, how they can be applied in the real-world situation, how your classroom learning prepares you for your better performance in the industry that you have to work on. So, you have to work on the content; at the same time you have to look at the application aspect of it. How are we going to apply this knowledge? How this concept is applied? So, you have to be aware and train yourself accordingly.  Then, work on your grooming. Little-little work on your grooming, the way you appear, your dress. The way you appear, some soft skills, body language you have work on. In the majority of the case, with my own experience, what we feel that the interview, interviewee we come in the room, unnecessarily becomes stiff. The body language is very stiff. You try to be very formal; body language is very stiff. You are stressed.  Or if body reflexes are not natural and normal, and this tension creates a lot of distraction and a lot of problems, stammering, or certain other problems. Be in control. And do not be scared of being rejected. You are going there for selection. So, rejection should not be a point of thinking in the mind. Do your best and believe that you can do justice to the job offered. With this belief you enter the room, work on your grooming; the dressing should be appropriate to the occasion. Usually, we have formal dress, but the color combination should be in contrast. And usually, light colored shirt with dark pant, formal shoes, and you should look well-groomed person, a cheerful person to work with. You should focus on positivity. And finally, arrange your papers and testimonials very meticulously. Because you may be asked to show any of the testimonials. So, whatever you have mentioned in your application and whatever you have mentioned in your CV, resume, please make sure that you carry all these testimonials in a folder with you.  Then we move to while-interview, the second phase of the entire process. So, you are actually into the interview room. You are actually facing the interview panel and there the actual performance happens. So, pre-interview is preparation before the performance, while-interview is the actual act of performance, you have to perform there. So, you have to make sure that you leave a good impression during your interview. And how you are going to do that? You need to speak intelligibly, speaking fluently, speaking confidently. You paraphrase; if you are not able to understand, paraphrase it. If you feel that your interviewer is not able to understand you, you paraphrase, you explain it in an alternative manner. Ask for clarifications if you do not get the question right. There are certain linguistic skills we have to keep in mind. We will shortly talk about it.  We will shortly talk about interactive skills. There are certain communication strategies we have to follow. We have to develop promptness in our responses, and arguments must be logical. So, with your tone, with your register, with your appearance and with your positivity, you can leave a very impressive and deep impact on your interviewers.  Post-interview, there are certain things that we need to follow up. You may be asked to complete certain other formalities in terms of documentation and testimonials, or possibly you may be asked to come for another round of interview. So, you have to keep an eye and take note of whatever developments happens inside the interview. You may be asked to wait for some time, and you may be asked for another round of discussion. So, you have to follow it up.  So, once you get out of the room, your interview is not over yet until you are officially told to leave. So, wait for that set of instructions and comply with the instructions you are given. So, this is the structure of an interview and these are the three stages.  So, we were talking about linguistic skills. Linguistic skills involve the accuracy of vocabulary. So, proper selection of words in your sentences, in your expression. Grammatical errors spoil the whole mood because they also reflect your competence in the language. Pronunciation, you do not have to sound like a Britisher or an American, you sound like the way you are, natural neutral ascent. You do not have to act, you do not have to try, just be whatever you are, but tempo must be appropriate, do not hurry, do not rush to answer. Relax and wait and formulate your ideas and answer. But your pronunciation must be intelligible. The pronunciation should not create confusion and misunderstanding of the meaning of it. Then you should work on the to develop your ability to handle, arrange your topics.  Always remember, in interviews, they do not ask you straight theories or a straight question. They give you a context; they give you a perspective about a certain technical idea and ask you to respond to it. So, you have to develop this art of communication, interaction, explaining things and multiple alternatives. So, you have to work on that, how to paraphrase, how to explain and range of context they create, you have to be able to understand the context and respond to that quickly.  And also, we need to avoid any kind of stereotype, any remark that never represents a stereotype. Any remark that talks about, tells you, tells them about your bias. So, all kinds of biases, all kinds of stereotypes, preferences, you should not show that you have a strong likings and disliking. It has to be tamed, and you need to sound balanced, you need to sound neutral.  Any kind of such signal and hint of your bias forces them to probe further, and they keep on asking further questions, and you are trapped. So, make sure that you do not make any categorical remark and answer. And finally, the cohesion of ideas. So, the ideas expressed in your answers must be cohesive, connected and related. We cannot afford to have disjoint ideas from our wild imaginations. They have to be grounded in a context, they have to be grounded in a situation that is appropriate and required for the moment.  Then we have certain interactive skills and that is not a one-way thing, we have to practice. It comes to you gradually, work on your fluency and speak at a natural speed. You should not be speaking too fast. At the same time, you should not be speaking too slow. In both cases, it is problematic. So, you have to practice and develop the rate of your speech at a neutral speed.  Then link the ideas, do the paraphrasing, come up with an alternative explanation if you feel that your interviewer is not able to understand you, explain it again in different words, different expressions. So, paraphrasing. You have to substantiate your answer with appropriate examples, and you may be given a chance to ask questions at the end of the interview. Do not lose that moment and be prepared to ask questions appropriate questions.  You cannot ask questions like, am I selected? Can you tell me whether I am selected? Can you tell me whether I performed better? Such questions are cliché questions. Do not show your desperate desire to know answers, but ask relevant questions which talks about your key observation and your professional skills. So, questions about the profile, job profile. Questions about your road map, your possibilities in their organization, questions about organization itself. So, you have to be ready with 2–3 questions in advance. When you are given a chance, you can ask your question and they would answer you.  And finally, we have certain communication strategies. First and foremost, the moment you enter the room, you have to be very polite, pleasant and greet everyone. The opening of your answer should be pleasing one, and it should begin with a positive note. Try to avoid criticizing any individual, be your teacher, be your older employer or anyone. Do not do any bad-mouthing about things. Do not show your strong opinion about things. Holding the floor means with your prompt answers, with your appropriate answers, you are in control and the interview goes in the desired direction. Paraphrasing we have been discussing. Clarify if you do not understand any question or ask for clarification if they do not understand any question, any answer that you have given; paraphrase it.  Body language should be appropriate in the sense that you should not look like shaky, you should not be tapping your finger while answering, swinging your legs while answering, sweating unnecessarily. Being anxious, your anxiety should not be reflected. Your body reflection should be normal and relaxed, posture should be normal and relaxed and that bears upon the overall confidence and performance that has bearing upon it. And interpreting the feedback appropriately. You might be answering some question and meanwhile another panel gives a perspective or feedback or a remark, do not jump to that. First, you evaluate it, complete your sentence and then address the person. So, you should not reply like a hurry to finish everything within no time.  Now, after looking at all these things, we realize that preparing for an interview is not a short term, shortcut way; it requires a lot of preparation, much before the interview happens. And from today, you can start working on your language, you can start working on pronunciation, you can start working on grooming, you can start developing the wide range of understanding of the topics, you can develop understanding wide range of themes and context.  You can work on applying your knowledge acquired knowledge into real-life practices and other professional skills, it is a gradual process. You can work on that and with that I believe that if you work on all these aspects and skills, you will be better prepared for interviews. We will try to bring you real life live interview in some of our videos very soon. So, take care and work hard, focus on these things, and we will meet in some other class with some more details. Thank you very much.

title: Context of Communication- The Speaking Model
text: English - II Professor Om Prakash Guest Faculty, Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Context of Communication-The Speaking Model Welcome to class. Today we are going to talk about the role of context, situation, location, space, time, participants in communication. So, how the context plays a crucial role in effective communication. This is what we are going to talk today. When we say ‘I know English’, when we say ‘I can communicate in English’, what d o we actually refer to? Are we talking about our command on vocabulary? So, knowledge of the words?
