So, here we are giving you a few examples. ‘All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players’, William Shakespeare said that. ‘I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life for the sheep’. ‘All our words are but crumbs that fell down from the feast of the mind’. ‘Let us be grateful to the people who make us happy, they are the charming gardeners w ho make our souls blossom.’  ‘And your very flesh shall be a great poem’. ‘Advertising is the rattling of the stick inside a swill bucket’. ‘Dying is a wild night and a new road’. ‘Fill your paper with the breathing of your heart’. So, these are things ta ken from different people, different writings. They have become metaphorical expressions in our lives. So, we use, we are giving you these metaphors to sit down with them, think about their meaning and see how we use them in different contexts.  Like sometimes people use metaphors in a formal context to make things impressive to, make to sound impressive. Here is a quote, one line quote from Kennedy's remarks in San Antonio, Texas, when he was dedicating the Aerospace Medical Center, and he said one sentence there that ‘America has tossed its cap over the wall of space’. So, this one sentence is metaphorical in nature in terms of claiming territory in the space. Not only claiming territory in the space, but being first in claiming that territory in the open wild space. So, though, as a politician, he was using this to justify expenses from tax dollars for a space research, but this is a politician's rhetoric to convince people, and it is like using your money for good. Space research is abstract in nature. It may not directly have much to do with the comfort in people that one can see. However, that is not true. Space, the advancement in space research has made our lives much easier. But initially, it is a very expensive affair, and it costs a lot of money, it takes a lot of energy.  So, a lot of times people use these kinds of metaphors, can also be called a figure of speech, for expressing themselves in emphatic way or making themselves emphatic.  So, another goal of the use of metaphor is to use your language, to make your language impressive, to make, to learn to use your language in a better way, as a tool for brighter success. So, to conclude the all I want to say, it is left to the user of the languages. Though, it takes the lot of efforts to learn metaphors of a new language, it is left to the users, whether we want to pick a metaphor in an informal situation or we want to pick a metaphor for the use in a formal situation.  In either case, it is going to be a tricky thing. It is related to pragmatics, it is related to language use, and we need to learn the rules of the language use at the same time, the rules that help us compute language in our mind to make it impressive. With that, we stop here. Take a quick look at these things, bring questions to us. And until we meet next time, take care. Bye, bye.

title: Negative Sensitive Elements in English
text: English-II Professor Rajesh Kumar Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Welcome to the class. Today, we are going to talk about the structure of English sentence once again. We are going to talk about the structure of English in the backdrop of learning language. We are going to mix a couple of things to show you specific details of structure in English. Furthermore, we are going to show you how it works, how the computation works, how these structures are processed in human mind, and they are unique, but they do not escape the processing of human mind. And when we understand them, when we look at them, when we appreciate their uniqueness and processing, underlying processing, we get to learn something very subtle about the structure of language, in particular, structure of English language. So, we are going to look at this, and we are going to see how they work. The element that we are going to look at today, these elements are called negative sensitive elements. There are some elements in English language which occur only when you have a negative sentence, in other words, only when you have a negative element in a sentence.  So, and we are going to show you the descriptions of that. Such elements do occur in other languages too. Such elements occur in the languages that you speak primarily as your first language. When we are done discussing these things, I invite you to think about your own language, to think about the languages that you speak effortlessly, language that you grew up speaking as a child. There is a reason for that. The reason why I am asking you to think about that is having looked at the structures that we are going to discuss today for English, when you compare and when you first you look at how these structures of English are processed in our mind, then you look at how such elements you learned effortlessly in your language without any specific attention.  When you look at this comparison, at this stage in learning for you, you are going to see this example, and you are going to learn this one. At the same time, other examples of such importance, other nuances of English structure of this type will come to your attention, and they will become easier for you to learn.  So, let us start with this. As we know, we learn language by looking at grammatical competence. That is, we understand structure through how it gets processed in our mind along with pragmatic competence. At some other point we will talk about pragmatic competence separately. But pragmatic simply means how we use the language.  So, there are certain constraints we apply in the use of language, and they are beyond grammar. They are not grammatical in nature, but they are very important because they go side by side with grammar. So, the main point is, the entire process of learning of language happens simultaneously with grammatical competence on one side and pragmatic competence on other side.  So, what this grammatical competence is? What is this grammatical competence? It is sometimes called simply competence, sometimes called linguistic competence, sometimes called I-language. They are all different names. They do have their specific meanings. But for the purpose of this class, I would request you to look at all these elements as language processing that happens internal to our mind.  At the same time, the term performance or linguistic performance or pragmatic competence or communicative competence or E-language, these are the terms for how we use language for understanding the rules in language use, how we use, how we learn the rules of language use. So, as we are saying, learning means both together, rules of language structure and rules of language use together. These two things together make language learning complete.  Having said that, we know that these are the elements that help us understand language as a unique thing, language as a unique capacity of humans, because learning of language is also a unique method. We learn language effortlessly as a child, but as a grownup adult, we have to put efforts in learning language. We are all trying to improve our English by putting in efforts, and hence it becomes important for us to pay attention to the things that are effortless, that are learned effortlessly as children and that makes language as a special endowment.  And this is the reason, because as a child we learn language effortlessly, this is the reason why sometimes it is said learning language is child’s play. So, the reason for that is, we need to know as given, that all normal human children are born to learn language. They are by birth equipped with language acquisition device and universal grammar within it for the which they use for the purpose of learning language and in which there are components of, hypothetical components of human mind. And as you see in this picture, language acquisition device as part of human mind is what is responsible for processing the input that comes to human mind which is very fuzzy, not targeted towards learning languages and limited in quantity. They come from immediate society, that is, the kinds of languages spoken around the child from the immediate society, family, relatives, etc. And as an output, same language comes out, but what gets guaranteed through the processing of this human mind is that the output is perfectly grammatical and infinite in nature. And thus, we speak the language. This does not quite work for adults, but what works is also part of it. Please hear me out carefully. This is an elaboration of how children learn. But how adults learn language, how grownups learn language follows from understanding this structure, this follows from what goes in learning as a child.  So, with this, children develop language as a generative system. Using their generative system they develop language as a capacity. And as we know, it miraculously develops. And this happens through the inbuilt hypothetical language acquisition device. This process is very fast for children, very effortless and requires no instruction.  And here is the key for us. Whatever that processing happens requires instruction for adults, meaning requires attention. It is not effortless, the way it is for children. Therefore, it requires efforts. And the processing is not as fast, but equal, not equally fast, but little slower than that, still very fast. So, efforts and instruction together is limited in the structural part. And this is the reason why we need to focus attention to structures.  So, as an example of this part, this discussion, as an example of how we focus, what we pay attention to, and how the processing works for us, we are going to look at negation and some negative sensitive elements in the structure of English, and I am going to put them in perspective in the for you to understand. So, we have seen the functioning of negation a little bit earlier.  So, let us refresh them. When a negative element appears in a sentence, it makes the sentence negative. So, let us go back and remind ourselves: the sentence has two parts, namely subject a d predicate. So, negation, and other than subject, everything is part of predicate. What we know in addition is, inside predicate, the most important part is the verb, because every other part of predicate is about the verb. So, within the predicate when negation occurs, it negates the whole sentence in a particular way. And so, the negation as part of the predicate negates the whole sentence and therefore, we say a sentence is negative. So, what are the negative words in English? We have ‘no’ and ‘not’, very simple, two specific negative elements in English. So, we can, we have a sentence like ‘John is a doctor ’. Look at this sentence. It is a very simple plain sentence. This is an affirmative sentence. When we say ‘John is not a doctor ’. This is a negative sentence. This ‘not’ is a negative word in this sentence and this whole sentence becomes negative because of that. What I invite you and what I remind you to invoke from your understanding is, negation always comes in a sentence around tense. So, when we look at tense and negation together, it gives us a very important understanding. It builds our understanding in an important way. How does that happen? Please look at that. See, we can take a sentence, ‘John likes novels’ or ‘story books’ or ‘movies ’. We are taking these examples only for the purpose of learning. So, please pay attention to the structural details that we are talking about. And then, having seen these things, we will apply this to the spoken language. This is an affirmative sentence. To make it a negative sentence, we need to bring in a negation element. And you will be surprised to see that the presence, so tense is part of this verb here. As you know, this is an affirmative sentence, but present tense. So, present tense somehow is embedded in this verb. To make it a negative sentence or when the sentence becomes negative, you will be surprised to see, this tense has to come out of the verb. So, in an affirmative sentence tense and verb are together, with each other. So, when a sentence becomes negative, when a sentence becomes, when a negation comes in a sentence, and it makes the sentence negative, here is how I want you to understand. The way verb and tense are, they are like this with one another. They have to separate from one another and negation has to come in between.  How? Look at the following example to understand. How do, what is the negative of this sentence, ‘John does not like novels ’. Please understand that. Like is the verb and here is the negation and here is your tense and number, that is present tense and singular number. So, this whole thing had to separate out of the verb for this to occur, which is not the case in an affirmative sentence.  In an affirmative sentence, number that is singular, because the subject is singular, and tense, present, they are all together on it. Number is visible with s and tense is not visible. But despite tense not being visible in an affirmative sentence, we need to separate it out, or it gets separated, that is a better way of saying, when a sentence becomes negative. So, a negation and a negative sentence or a sentence which were negation makes the sentence negative is an important thing to pay attention to. Same thing happens in the past tense. You have seen this before. This was just to remind your memory. So, if we said, ‘John liked novels ’, and we want to make it a negative sentence, you have to say, ‘did not like ’. So, this becomes past and this is your verb and negation comes in between. In short, for negation to occur in a sentence, tense has to separate from the verb. It is not just in a statement, what we need to know and what we want to pay attention to is, in a sentence negation occurs in between tense and verb. So, the order of elements in a sentence is tense, negation, verb and then objects. That is the important part. So, this is about negation.  Now, this is about affirmative and negative sentences. What next I want you to see is, there are certain elements in English sentence which can occur only when a sentence is negative, not when sentence is affirmative. Let us look at those sentences.  We call them negative sensitive elements. And they are not something that we do not know about. I am just trying to bring your attention to these things. You have already used these things 100 times, but I want you to look at these elements afresh to see the beauty of structural description and, for understanding nuances of structure of English language. You will appreciate structural nuances in a better way by looking at these things. So, look at these things. Terms like anybody, anyone or anything, or just for that matter just any, these are some of the negative sensitive elements. So, when we say anybody or anyone, it is plus animate or when we say anything, it is minus animate, meaning plus animate means it is used for living things, minus animate means it is used for non-living things.  So, the so anybody has another counterpart, somebody. So, somebody or someone or something, these are not negative sensitive elements, not sensitive to negation. Meaning, these elements can occur in a sentence without negation also in affirmative sentences, but not these. Likewise, we have some elements like a word with a special meaning, a penny. I am going to show you these things in a moment these two, but let us first look at anybody, anyone, anything or any.  Let us look at these examples. When we say ‘John did not like anything ’, look at this, we can never say ‘John liked anything’. This is not a good sentence in English. And therefore, I am putting a star here. Not good means ungrammatical. What it means is for anything to be used in this sentence, this sentence must be a negative sentence. So, the presence of this word ‘anything’ is contingent upon ‘not’, negative element in the sentence. And see this, this is a past tense, tense is already separated. Here is the verb, here is tense and here is negative thing and this is negative sensitive. So, anything, you know the meaning of this sentence, but all I am adding to this nuanced structural description is ‘anything’ is a negative sensitive element in English language, because it can only occur with negation in a negative sentence in English. ‘Mary did not meet with anyone ’. Look at this. It is contingent again upon this ‘not’. This is tense, this is negation, this is the verb, because we cannot say ‘Mary met with anyone ’. This is not a good sentence in English. We can say ‘Mary met with someone ’. Therefore, we said, remember, someone, somebody, something, these are not negative sensitive elements. So, we can say, ‘Mary met with someone ’, but we can never say, ‘Mary met with anyone ’. That is not possible in English. What does this mean? What is the meaning of not possible? It means, very simple thing. It means ‘anyone’ can occur in a sentence only with negation. And as you know, any is just, it is ‘any’ which is making, this is how we combine anybody, anyone, anything to make it plus animate or minus animate.  So, I hope this becomes clearer to you in understanding what we mean by negative sensitive element, and how one is contingent, how these elements are contingent upon dependent on negative elements in English sentence. Think about more sentences like these. Think about sentences where you can use them without negation. And I am going to show you the context where they can be used without negation, but in very restrictive environments, and you will see that.  Before that, please look at some more examples. We can say, ‘AJU did not speak a word ’. Look at this phrase ‘a word ’. Here, a word does not mean literally one word. Here, metaphorically it means anything or nothing. So, again, this one, this element can only be used with that meaning in a negative sentence. We can say ‘AJU spoke a word ’, but here a word means literally one word. With ‘anything’ interpretation, it can only be used in a negative sentence. ‘Marita did not give a penny ’. We can say, to, let us say, to beggars. Sometimes beggars ask us for something. ‘Marita did not give a penny to beggars ’. We can say this metaphor as a penny or a red cent. This is an American phrase. Cent is a unit of money. It is the smallest unit of money, which means one, its equivalent to our one pies.  So, here also the interpretation is nothing or anything. Meaning, these things can only occur when you have negation in the sentence. If you use them, then it means literally a penny, meaning if you use them without negation, then it means literally a penny or a cent. It does not carry the same interpretation. So, some elements like anything, anybody or anyone, a red cent, a penny, there are some other elements, ‘at all ’. We have to say, ‘Marita did not speak at all ’. We cannot say, ‘Marita spoke at all’. So, these elements are sensitive to negation. These are, therefore, it is important for us to pay attention to these nuances.  We can, we do find one context, where these elements can occur without negation, but that context is unique, and they can only come if the sentence is a question sentence. We can say, ‘Did you meet with anyone? ’ Look at this sentence. There is no negation. But it is a question sentence. ‘Did you get a penny? ’ We can say that.  So, anyone type of negative sensitive element can occur with question sentence, but a penny type of or a word type of negative sensitive element cannot occur even in question sentence. So, these two need negation only to occur. These ‘anyone's’ need negation or question. So, here we, here I stop with this discussion and I want you to keep this unique structure in mind as our discussion on nuances of structure of English sentences, understanding particular grammatical pattern where we use certain sensitive elements with negation. We need to pay attention to these elements to understand the processing of these things and learning of these things. Now, as I mentioned in the beginning, I invite you to pay attention to these kinds of elements in the languages that you speak. Make a list of those elements, compare them with the elements, negatives, negative sensitive elements of English, compare them with negative sensitive elements of English and see how you learn these elements effortlessly when you acquired you are language as first language and that will give you an insight into why we need to pay attention to that process of learning in order for us to learn these things in a new language when we are making efforts to learn these things. Without putting in efforts, without paying attention to these processes, we would not get to the detailed nuances of these structures. And therefore, it is important for us to see these things. Hope this was useful, helpful to you. Please do the exercises that I have mentioned here. Please do the pattern analysis, pattern comparison between your language and English. And we look forward to your comments and discussion on these types. See you next time until then, bye-bye.

title: Pragmatic Competence Vs Communicative Confidence
text: English-II Professor Rajesh Kumar Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Welcome to the class. Today, we are going to talk about certain aspects of language learning.  There are certain things about language learning that teachers must know, that practitioners, professionals dealing with language teaching and language learning must know.  In this class, we are going to talk about those things to you primarily because we thought even learners must know about these things. We have been practicing these things as an underlying theme, as current underlying this course for helping you learn or improve your English. Therefore, at this stage, we decided that we will talk about these things to you so that you can see, evaluate, understand and apply them to your own learning hereafter. You have gone through a lot of things about learning in language. You know a lot of things about learning. In this class, we are talking about learning of English language.  We want to talk to you with examples about the things that help us improve our language. We need to understand how to improve our accuracy. Accuracy comes from understanding structure, and it is accuracy alone in learning English in particular or for that matter, learning any language in general, what gives us confidence if we need to sound confident, if we need to sound impressive in a language that we are learning, we are improving for ourselves. One key factor in that effort is accuracy. Only with maintaining accuracy, we are going to sound confident. This is undisputed fact. We want to understand now, we have been, we know very well that we need to learn a new language to communicate with people, those who speak that language. Namely, if I know English well, then I communicate with English speakers, that is, anybody who speaks English well. To do so, I need to keep my own language accurate, my own language impressive, through my accuracy. This is undisputed. In order to move through that facet, we believe it will help to add understanding of pragmatic competence with communicative competence for achieving communicative confidence. So, we have been talking about communicative competence. Today, we are going to bring in communicative competence, language competence along with pragmatic competence, and we will tell you about these things. And to put all these things together, we are working on building communicative confidence. You can find three terms communicative competence, linguistic competence and pragmatic competence in literature if you read about them. However, communicative confidence is my term that I have developed in my practice of research and teaching. It simply means communicative competence, linguistic competence and pragmatic competence together builds communicative confidence for the learners of a target language. So, let me move and tell you about it.  In the process of language learning, what is it that is of paramount significance? It involves two parts. One is grammatical competence, and communicative competence. It is grammatical competence, namely grammatical accuracy, which comes from understanding subconscious computation in our mind, which is known as linguistic competence. So, the terms like linguistic competence, grammatical competence, they mean the same thing or when we say computation in our subconscious, they all mean the same thing. We need to add pragmatic competence with that which are important for learning of language, learning a new language. So until now, we have been building linguistic competence in English. And now, today, we are going to bring in elements of pragmatic competence to help you build it further hereafter. I want to add here that these two parts, linguistic competence that is grammatical competence, grammatical accuracy as well as pragmatic competence, function together. Linguistic competence in literature is also known as I-language. I-language means internal language, the language that is internal to human mind. In other words, again the it refers to the subconscious processing, subconscious computation of language. And the other term is performance, which is also known as E-language, that is, external language, that is, the language that we use to communicate. So, this distinction is subtle and all we need to know about this distinction is language internal to human mind is something that we have not used so far. That is, we have not started speaking. The moment we start speaking, that becomes E-language. So, hopefully, this distinction is clear to you. We are only saying that the two needs to come together, only then we learn the target language.  We need to put them together and then it works. It works for learning. Learning of language includes aspects of both. We are going to show you some examples from English and Hindi, in particular, and then you can look at examples from languages that you speak and contrast and compare them with English examples to see whether what we are going to tell you make sense or not and see how that helps in your own learning, whether understanding about these things has any contribution in learning or not. You will be judged for that.  So, we will talk about few things related to that. At this point, we need to know some of the scholars who have talked about these things in literature. There is a very famous person who has worked on language from the perspective of learning, acquisition and education. He is M.A.K Halliday.  In a very famous paper in 1993, he points out that when we learn language, that is, the process of learning of languages, is not simply engaging in one kind of learning among man;, rather they are learning the foundation of learning itself. That is, the onto genesis of languages is at the same time the onto genesis of learning. In short, if we want to understand that, he is trying to say understanding the embedded process of learning language is also about learning the process of learning itself. Therefore, he says, learning of language, that is, when we learn language, this understanding, this process is not just understanding one among many things that we learn.  We learn many things in our lives. We learn to speak, we learn to swim, walk, cycle, drive car, some people learn to fly a plane, some people learn to cook, dance, music, singing. So, learning language is not just one among all other kinds of learning. What he says, learning languages is making an effort to, trying to understand underlying aspects of language learning is one, not just one among much other learning, rather it is learning about learning itself. I hope this is clear. This is just a this part is just to tell you how important it is to understand how we learn. In particular, how we learn language.  We know that we are watching structural aspects of language. We have looked at several nuanced aspects of different structural patterns in English. If you calculate your experience of learning so far, you are going to say what Mark Trimming in Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy says about language. It is ‘language is an impressive and fascinating human capacity and language, human languages are strikingly powerful and complex systems ’. It is not just, when you understand this, we begin to believe that it is not possible to learn the underlying structural nuances by practicing, parroting, that is, practicing like your parrot, that is not possible. We only need, the only thing that works for learning of language, either as a child or as an adult, is when we understand the nuanced pattern, nuances of underlying patterns of language, then we understand how it works, how it functions, and such understanding starts showing impact yielding when we speak the language. This, there is no alternative to this. Understanding this has dramatic impact on learning. We have been telling you these things time to time. Today, we are talking about that systematically, and we are going to show you just some examples on the basis of that.  So, look at the following things that some other scholars have talked about language, for example, Charles Darwin. Charles Darwin says, ‘man has instinctive tendency to speak as we see in the babbles of our children, while no child has instinctive tendency to bake, brew and write ’. Please note the distinctions that he is, that Darwin is talking about. He is saying ‘instinctive tendency to speak ’. This is the fundamental capacity that we are born with. He is talking about, this ‘instinctive’ is related to our cognition. It is related to our mind. So, he is talking about when it comes to speak, it is about human mind. And he says that we notice that right from the beginning, children start to babble when they have not even started speaking sounds. Even the babbling tells you that children are, the newly born baby is going to speak. While, whereas we do not see such instinctive tendency among children to bake, brew and write: very carefully picked up activities that children get involved with in learning. Remember, just now, we were talking about Halliday. Halliday says learning to understand about language. Understanding what goes in language learning tells us that language learning is not one among many learnings. The language is unique, language learning is unique, other things are not, and he puts, Darwin puts them, to bake is one kind of learning; to brew coffee; to make cake is one; to brew coffee is one and to write is another one. So, please keep in mind, learning to speak is different from learning to write.  When we talk about language learning, we talk about skills like speaking, reading, writing, reading. We talk about four skills, LSRW: listening, speaking, reading and writing. Among these, writing is very different, reading and writing are connected. Because once you know how to write, you also learn to read and the other way around. Point is, speaking is very different from writing, as even Charles Darwin say s. We know there are thousands people, thousands of speakers of all languages of the world who speak but do not write. It never happens that you know how to write, but you do not speak the language. Language speaking is instinctive. Speaking is genetically designed. Human beings are genetically designed to speak natural language, whereas we need to learn additionally to write. Therefore, what we come to conclude as language is, one of the language is the most sophisticated activity of human mind. Among many other activities that human mind performs, language is one of the most complex and sophisticated activities that happens in a human mind. Therefore, paying attention to its computation is crucial. I keep underlining this so many times. I aim to hammer it so that we do not skip those patterns and the development. However, what is crucial in building this capacity of language is input from our society. That is, we need to hear, we need to train our ears with the sounds which will work as input for the purpose of learning. The more input we provide through our ears in our mind, the processing becomes faster, and they yield the results in a faster way. This part is again a very significant part for all of you to keep in mind.  Next, when we move, for a long time, learning of language was really considered a pattern drill situation, stimulus and response activity. It was like, we hear something, and we practice that, and we learn to speak. This was a long term scientific understanding and long term scientific belief. This is also known as psychological foundation of understanding language. Whereas, in 1957, Chomsky brought in certain ideas and that changed our understanding of the entire process of language learning. And he asked certain epistemological questions and these questions, some of the questions that come out of his work are listed here. What constitutes our knowledge of language? That is, when we become speaker of a language, what constitutes that knowledge? How is that knowledge acquired? He is particularly talking about children. Let us keep in mind that we are talking about learning languages for adults. That is, you are making an attempt to learn and improve your English as a target language as an adult. Chomsky was talking about learning or acquisition of language for children, very, very nascent infants, early, early acquisition for children. You know that by four or five years after birth, children start speaking the target language, the language from the immediate society. So, and it is understanding that process, uncovering that process and applying some of them to the process of learning for adults is going to help us in learning; that is what we have been trying to do for you. So, he asked the questions that what constitutes that knowledge. How is that, what constitutes the knowledge? How is that knowledge acquired? And how is that knowledge put in practice? What is it? How is it acquired? And how is it put in practice? That is, how we develop it here in our mind and then how we start using them. Chomsky is asking for children, how do children acquire, and how do they put to use? The underlying theme of entire research in Chomsky's paradigm is that. So, he brings in certain aspects, and we will talk about some of them to you and that becomes the foundation of understanding language for children. We take, we pick things up from there and see how many of them are applicable for learning as an adult. And this is what we are putting in to understand the third part, third question is applicable. Christian third question is applicable for adults also. That is, how is this acquired knowledge put in practice?  So, we understand that initial impression of a stimulus and response. As you know, stimulus is, we give something and response is when we take it out. So, input and output, that is, response is equivalent to stimulus or output is equivalent to input that theory was rejected. That is, language learning is a matter of habit formation was rejected. Meaning, it does not work merely through practice. Therefore, language is not merely a matter of habit formation. What happens in learning is, this computation of language, is part of generative mechanism, that is, is part of human mind. This computation happens in human mind. This is the part which psychologists missed which Chomsky brought in. So, here, the point is when we hear, when we talk to people, we keep telling you to listen to news, to read books, to read, to spend half an hour time in reading and listening. Now, you can see why we say that. We are saying that, because that that will work as input for you. That is going to be imperfect, that imperfect simply means it is not directed towards learning. It is fuzzy. Meaning again, it is not very clear. So, imperfect and fuzzy stimulus will yield perfect learning. It does yield to perfect learning for kids. We hope that some parts of it will yield to perfect learning for grown up adults as well. And therefore, we talk about language computation, which is generative mechanism of human mind.  So, as a child we develop knowledge of language from that computation. And that is, children automatically derive underlying rules that we are making effort to learn. And that happens through the computational mechanism for children. They do it in a subconscious process. We need to do it through conscious process. Therefore, we need to know about those mechanisms.  So, when we try to understand the knowledge of language, it is a technical term, and we can define it, that it consists, it is about underlying rules that we know, but we do not know that we know them. This is about first language learning. So, we do not know that we know all the rules of our first language.  In English, in learning of English, we need to uncover those rules that we know to learn them in a conscious fashion to help us produce so that when we learn these underlying rules, we can produce sentences, and we can enable ourselves to separate grammatical sentences from ungrammatical patterns, from ungrammatical ones, and that will result into speaking grammatical sentences.  So, now, I want to give you some examples of that. So, you see, let me talk about two examples from Hindi, two nuanced examples that is that children learn without any specific instruction. All of us learn without knowing what we are learning. And these things we need to underline for learning English. In English, about English we need to underline these things. So, let us first understand. I am going to describe two sentences to you in Hindi. Please look at this slide carefully. And you will get the point, the main point underlying these two sentences even if you do not understand Hindi. I am using Hindi only as an example. So, please see. I am not writing anything in Hindi on this slide. I am using phonetic, sort of phonetic transcription for explaining these things to you. So, the first sentence is ‘AJU KE PAAs do batch main.’ You ask any speaker of Hindi, if you are one, you check it for yourself. If you are not, ask any speaker of Hindi. ‘AJU KE PAAs do batch main’ is not a good sentence. Therefore, we have put these star marks here, that means, not grammatical. But if we say ‘AJU KE do batch main,’ that is a good sentence. But, so AJU has two kids. This is an English sentence that we want to say, AJU has two kids. In Hindi, we say the same thing, ‘AJU KE do batch main.’ We do not say, ‘AJU KE PAAs do batch main.’ You see how you read this. This first word is AJU, this ‘KE’ is a possessive pronoun, ‘KE PAAs’ is also possessive pronoun, ‘do’ means two, ‘batch’ means kids, ‘main’ is are; literally meaning two kids are near, this ‘KE PAAs’ literally means near in the sense of belonging. So, we say ‘two kids are near AJU ’, meaning, ‘AJU has two kids ’. But ‘KE PAAs’ as a post position cannot be used in this sentence. Otherwise, the sentence becomes ungrammatical. We can only us eke, ‘AJU KE do batch main.’  Look at the second sentence. We can say, ‘AJU KE PAAs do Gabriela main.’ Look at this again, AJU, this ‘KE PAAs’ is possessive pronoun, ‘do’: two, ‘cars’: Gabriela, ‘main’: are. So, ‘main’: are, ‘Gabriela ’: cars, ‘do’: two. So, AJU has, when we want to say AJU has two cars, we have to say, ‘AJU KE PAAs do Gabriela main ’, not ‘AJU I do Gabriela HAI ’. What are we, what do we watch. When we see these two English sentences, ‘AJU has two kids’ and ‘AJU has two cars ’, we see in both the sentences we are using has as auxiliary and sentence has similar patterns. But in Hindi, the structure of sentence makes a distinction between two markers depending upon what we are talking about having. If we are talking about having two kids, we have a different post position. If we are having about, talking about having two cars, then we have a different post position.  In other words, what we are talking about having with AJU has implications for grammatical structure in Hindi, not in English. Likewise, there are so many things in English which are not applicable to Hindi or for that matter, the language that you speak. What we speak as our first language has the lot of implications for our learning of a new language. So, if we are aware of these distinctions, we do not need to know every single distinction, but if we are aware of these distinctions, then we end up becoming a better learner, a better speaker. Then the rule will apply, the more we know, the better a speaker we are. This is what we mean when we say learning language includes acquisition of inbuilt socio-cultural context.  So, we not only need to know grammatical patterns, we not only need to know grammatical patterns for attaining accuracy; to attaining higher degree of accuracy, we need to know inbuilt socio-cultural context. It is not a complex thing. It is a very simple thing. Like I said, take these two Hindi sentences, talk to any Hindi speaker, if you are not the one yourself, and you will get to find out without effort any Hindi speaker we will say these things to you, that is inbuilt socio-cultural context is already developed in them as the speaker of that language. So, naturally what follows is if we want to become a better speaker of a new language, namely English, then we need to develop not only accuracy for grammatical patterns, but also for inbuilt socio-cultural stuff. For example, we need to know that this ‘KE PAAs’ or ‘KE’ distinction is not applicable in English. We are fine in saying AJU has two cars or AJU has two kids. They are fine.  That is not to say speakers of English do not make a distinction between kids and cars. In Hindi, we make a distinction between kids and cars in our language structure. But in English this distinction is made in human cognition, but not in this structure. That is the point that we need to know about: the differences between our languages and the new language, the target language, namely English, that we are learning here.  Let me tell you another example of similar sort. Again, two very simple sentences from Hindi and see how they compare and contrast with Hindi and what is it that we learn from these two sentences and how we make best use of this understanding for learning English. When we say, ‘AJU Adam chantey HAI ’, check with a Hindi speaker. Some speakers of Hindi will tell you, there does not seem to be anything wrong with this sentence, but nobody speaks like this. The way people speak this sentence is, ‘AJU KO Adam chalice ’. So, ask somebody, I want to say a sentence in Hindi. ‘AJU wants a pen ’. How do we say that sentence in Hindi and you, if you speak a language other than Hindi, check your own language. In Hindi, we say AJU wants a pen as ‘AJU KO Adam chalice ’, which literally means AJU needs a pen. So, in Hindi, the distinction between want and need, that is, required, is very critical. Hindi speakers, cognitively speaking, do not want to express desire in the form of want for worldly objects. Hear me out carefully. There is nothing ungrammatical about sentence number three. But this looks odd, because it uses a verb, want, ‘chantey HAI ’. The same sentence becomes good if you replace ‘Adam ’. So, ‘Adam’ is an example of a worldly object. Take any object, ‘Adam chantey HAI ’, ‘keypad chantey HAI ’, ‘pies chantey HAI ’, they are not good. They are not suitable in this sentence. But if you use anything else other than these objects, then the sentence is going to be good. You can say ‘AJU Jana chantey HAI ’. That is perfectly fine. ‘AJU Khan chantey HAI ’, ‘AJU piney chantey HAI ’. We do not say that usually in Hindi. That is another thing which I will use as a footnote here and discuss some other time. It is a unique thing about world's languages that ‘piney’ is a transitive verb. But if you drop the object from the sentence then it, the absence of object in the context of ‘piney’ that is, drinking refers to alcohol. So, if you say, ‘AJU piney chantey HAI ’, that means AJU wants to drink alcohol. And if you do not want your sentence to mean that, you need to specify, what ‘piney chantey HAI ’, wants to drink what? So, you have to say, AJU wants to drink juice or AJU wants to drink water or AJU wants to drink milk or whatever you want you need to specify it, because in the absence of it, it means drinking. That is an additional point and that works for all the languages of the world, not just English, that not just Hindi, it works the same way in English. You can say ‘AJU wants to drink ’. Unless you specify the object in English too, it refers to drinking alcohol. So, that is the similarity between the two. But we were talking about difference, and we are trying to make a different point. We are saying, if the object is immaterial things, like ‘Jana ’, ‘Anna’, ‘Khan ’, ‘Deanna ’, ‘piney’, then the sentence is fine. ‘AJU far Jana chantey HAI ’, ‘AJU dinner Khan chantey HAI ’, ‘AJU juice piney chantey HAI ’, ‘AJU movie Deanna chantey HAI ’, ‘AJU son chantey HAI ’, ‘AJU Batman chantey HAI’, all those things are fine, but ‘AJU Adam chantey HAI’ is not good, ‘AJU pies chantey HAI’ is not good, ‘AJU GAAR chantey HAI’ is not good. If you say, ‘GAAR Karina chantey HAI ’, then it is fine. Now, the point is, what explains this nuanced difference between Hindi and English? Hindi speakers — this is my explanation, it may not match with yours or anybody else, but I invite you to check — and my explanation is, particularly for Hindi speakers, Hindi speakers do not want to express their desire. They do not want to verbalize their desire in direct sentences. So, how does it work? They convert it as a requirement. So, they will say, ‘AJU KO Adam chalice ’, meaning AJU needs a pen and that, for that there is a different verb that is used in Hindi which is ‘chalice ’. ‘Chalice’ is a frozen verb in Hindi. It does not change according to tense of the sentence, and it is an indirect sentence because there is a post position KO right after AJU. So, AJU, there is no agreement between this and this verb. So, whether it is ‘AJU KO Adam chalice’ or ‘Marita KO Adam chalice’ or ‘Ran KO Adam chalice ’, it is the same. The gender of the subject will not have anything to do with the verb. Verb is frozen and it is an indirect expression. It is a technique of making it a requirement. So, in Hindi, we want to say, I want, but we convert it into need. That is the only way to say this thing in Hindi. Having explained this to you for Hindi, I want to say this pattern is not applicable for English. We can simply say ‘AJU wants money ’, ‘AJU wants a shirt ’, ‘AJU wants a pen’ or ‘AJU wants to go ’, ‘AJU wants to drink ’, ‘AJU wants to sleep ’, ‘AJU wants to eat ’. All those things are possible in Hindi. I am sorry, all those things are possible, all those structures are possible in English. And we can also say in terms of requirements in English, ‘AJU needs a pen ’. So, ‘AJU wants a pen’ or ‘AJU needs a pen ’: this distinction is possible in two different sentences in English, but it works in a very different way in Hindi. I am sure it works in different ways in many other languages, but due to time, I am unable to discuss examples from other languages. However, I invite you to look at examples from other languages for yourself. So, my point is through these two examples for sentences, a set of two sentences for two different examples that I have given you, we need to know a lot about socio-cultural context, embedded meaning, embedded structure, embedded patterns to see nuances of a structure and embedded socio-cultural context of our own language as to learn a new language.  I have discussed this before, but I will bring this example again to you. ’ Gear AAO ’. If we want to say ‘far AAO ’, come home, it is not necessary, when we use imperative sentences. Imperative sentences are called request and orders. A sentence becomes a request or an order depending upon the context, again socio-cultural context, social context, and we need to know that. So, when we say ‘far AAO’ to a friend, we are not necessarily ordering a friend. It is a quite decent invitation. It is a quite decent expression without any order as a request to a friend or to an acquainted person whom we can use an informal sentence in that context. However, the formal counterpart of this sentence in Hindi is ‘far piece ’, which means ‘please come home ’. It is a higher degree for the first imperative, number five. In this one the subject is ‘tum’, in this one the subject is ‘AAP’ and that is the distinction between informal and formal. So, basically, we are saying five number, example number five is informal and example number six is formal.  We need to know this distinction not in terms of order and request, because five is not necessarily an order and six is not necessarily a request. You change the context. If you are the boss, and you tell even your junior employee a formal sentence, ‘KAL surah mile ’, this is not a request for that employee. For that employee, it is an order. So, when interpreting socio-cultural context in a given language, we need to know the embedded context of that language. At the same time, we need to learn the same thing for the target language as well. So, and it works the same way in English too. When we talk to an employee and say, ‘please see me tomorrow in the morning ’, that is not simply a request, meaning that does not give an option to that employee. At the same time, if I say, ‘see me tomorrow’ to a friend, it is not an order. So, the context tells us a lot. And the point that I am trying to make here is, learning about the context happens simultaneously with learning about structural nuances and these two things work together which we need to pay attention to.  We need to talk about one more example with you which is, which comes from the context of negation, and I am again using few Hindi sentences for you, hopefully it will become clearer. Look at sentence number seven, it says, ‘alone Kara AAP ice-cream kharidenge ’, you said, you will buy ice-cream. So, this is a sentence in Hindi. This is word by word meaning in the second sentence, the first sentence is Hindi, second sentence is word by word meaning and third is English. So, one is Hindi and third is English and two is meaning, word- by-word.  So, it says, you said you will buy me an ice-cream. So, number seven I have brought in just to build the context. So, keep this number seven sentence in mind. In response to number seven, if I say as number eight, ‘Maine key Kara ?’ That is, when did I say? This ‘when did I say ’, though it is a question sentence, it means in this context, ‘I did not say so ’. Meaning, ‘I did not say I will buy ice-cream ’. So, look at the look at this discourse competence. This is called pragmatic competence that a learner develops in the process of learning, which is important to build the context and that comes from the situation like this. We are actually using a question sentence, when did I say. Meaning, I did not say so.  So, there is another level, another layer here. In response to the sentence, ‘alone Kara AAP ice-cream kharidenge ’, we do not want to say, I did not say so, meaning, we do not want to refute somebody’s expectation. We refute the expectation by converting the sentence into a question, ‘when did I say?’ Meaning, I did not say so.  Also, we can say, ‘Maine Khan Kaseya? ’ Literally means, ‘where did I say?’ Implication is, I did not say so. So, to imply what we want to say sometimes we use a different structure, namely questions here. So, if you see this implication, it is an important topic. It is a big thing in language how we imply that is what we mean, we way something, that is, we use a particular type of sentence. We could possibly mean something else by saying that sentence. Somebody says, ‘let us go watch a movie today ’. If I say, ‘I have to go shopping ’. In response to, ‘let us go watch a movie today ’, if I say, ‘I have to go shopping ’, it is not an information to hearer that I have to go shopping. The hearer may not be interested in my act of shopping or the types of shopping. It is a very different kind of information to the hearer which implies ‘no’. We use this as a marker of politeness instead of saying no.  ‘No, I cannot go ’. To avoid that which sounds confrontational, negative, we use in strategy of giving another kind of information which hearer interprets from the knowledge of the context very clearly that the answer is ‘no’ and nobody makes this mistake. This is applicable in English too.  So, to conclude this part, we are, the purpose of this discussion with you is to understand that building grammatical competence, understanding nuances of patterns and understanding nuances of pattern for grammatical accuracy in speaking has to come along with pragmatic competence and only then, we get successful in building communicative confidence for us in the target language. Just wanted to describe few examples through these patterns, with these theoretical nuances for you to take a look at these things. I am sure this is going to be useful to you. As I said in the beginning, usually these things are important for teachers to keep in mind, but I believe it helps learners to see what is the embedded theme of the entire discussion and when you know these things inside out categorically, as an obvious thing to you, maybe it will yield, it will add to better learning and improving of English which is one of the targets of this course. I am sure it will work in that direction. Thank you so much.

title: Innovation in Vocabulary
text: English – II Professor Rajesh Kumar Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Welcome to the class. Today, we are going to talk about some innovative processes in building vocabulary. When I say vocabulary, I do not simply mean building a stock of words for us to use. Vocabulary is of course, it contains that, it contains lexical items that we use, but the process involved in building vocabulary includes a lot more than that. As you can pay attention to, it is about the process, and the process is almost similar to that of what we have been discussing structures. If we pay attention to the process, and if we pay attention to how these processes function in the subconscious of our mind, we get to understand a lot about the process involved in building the vocabulary in process in the making of words.  We are going to do that, but that is one part of it.  The second part, which is going to be the running theme, underlying theme, is there is a heavy role of sociocultural context in building vocabulary, in the making of words that we use in our regular life, or sometimes we use words from selective domains, from different domains to make our language either impressive or enriched. Either way, it is part of a process, and I wish to discuss a few things about that with you. So, when we talk about context, we know that contexts are culturally dependent. So, the process of making vocabulary that we use in India, that people can use in different parts of India, they are going to vary on geographical base. We are going to differ in terms of our uses, but more or less, you will find a running theme in that.  So, we have categorized this process in four, five domains, and we are going to talk about that, but please remember socio-culturally embedded context is important, and in this I would like to simplify this phrase for you. When we say socio-culturally embedded context we mean society, culture and context.  The three work together. They are intertwined.  We cannot look at culture out of society or society out of culture, and the context is embedded within that as well. So, the use of language in society is undoubtedly dependent on the cultural context.  So, the linguistic competence being one part, that is, what is possible and what is not possible is one part of this discussion, but the context embedded in society and culture has a lot to do with how we make words and how those words become either high frequency words for use in the society or low frequency words for use in the society or in our day today languages, in our spoken language. The other part which is important for us to keep in mind is the whole process of language use per se. It is also dependent on the context, in the sense that whether the context is formal or informal. We pick words from different areas, depending upon formal and informal nature of the use of language. So, all these things play a huge role in the back of our mind when we either make the word or use them. We are going to look at some of them to see.  One very productive pattern for word formation is adding prefixes or suffixes from ancient sources or resources. English has a very productive pattern of word formation using prefixes from Greek and Latin. These are classical, classic languages, classical languages. Both Greek and Latin have ancient connection with English, and they have borrowed, that is, English has borrowed a lot from them, from these two languages among many others. So, we are only going to look at a few things to indicate the process to you.  So, in this discussion I am not aiming at giving you a list of a whole range of words. Rather I intend to talk about the process and then that will be useful to you in helping yourself see this pattern and find this pattern in words that you use. So, look at this, there are some prefixes that we often find in words and then these are prefixes and suffixes from Greek and Latin sources, so they become low frequency words in our language.  So, we have words like look at this. Like let us look at first examples, aerobic or aeronautics. The first part that you see ‘aero’ comes from Greek prefix ‘are’ which means air, and that can be combined with other words to make a new word like aerobic, aerobics or aeronautics. Similarly, if you look at the other prefix ‘geo’, which means earth or related to earth, and then we get words like geometry, geopolitical, geography and so on. The whole word geography is from this prefix geo, which is Earth, are related to Earth.  ‘Semi’ means half and words like hemisphere comes from this prefix. ‘Herb’ it is related to, it is a word, it is a prefix, which means, literally means related to plants, and then we get words like herbivorous or herbal, or it is a prefix that you find in more words. It is a very productive pattern. ‘Hydro ’, it is water or related to waters, means, hydrogen, hydrochloride. When you use these words, when you see these words ‘hydrogen ’, the first part of this word hydro is a prefix, which means something related to water. ‘Hydrochloride ’, these are the names, this is the name of a chemical, ‘hydro project’ and more words with ‘hydro’ in: hydrogen, hydrochloride, hydroperoxide, hydro project, and so this indicates a productive pattern to us.  ‘Hyper ’: it means more or in excess. So, in words like hyperactive, hypersensitive; when you see this word hyperactive this prefix has a specific meaning, it is coming from another language, and we get words made of these prefixes and these words become low frequency words plus the moment you have words with low frequency, that is, words that occur lower in its frequency the number of times we use, they are also going to be high cognitive, in the high cognitive zone.  So, the higher the cognitive level, the lower the frequency, this is a very simple tool. So, all these words that you see are low frequency because they are higher in cognitive level. Why higher? Because they come from different sources.  ‘Hypo ’: hyperthermia, hypothyroidism. Just looking at the name, it is going to Eco me low frequency and the important part is, even if these are low frequency words, it is important for us to understand that there are prefixes from other languages, and once we understand these prefixes, the meaning of these words become easier for us, and above all, they cannot be, we cannot avoid these words in English languages and more in the domain of academic English, more in the domain of English from a specific field, the use of words in specific fields, and we quite often run across these words.  Some more are like ‘inter’, which means between. So, internet, interpersonal, these are some of the words that you can say.  ‘Intra’ which means within. So, intracellular, intranet, intracellular, int independent, there are a lot of words that you will find with these things. ‘Mega ’; these are common. It means big, so megabyte or mega star or mega performance. W e use this with quite a number of words in English, and we find it very regular. So, ‘re’ means back or again. Things like redo, reuse, rebuild, these are some of the recycle, these are some of the words where we use these prefixes. ‘Ultra’ is, the literal meaning of this word, is in excess of. So, ultrasonic, ultraviolet, ultrasensitive, ultrasound. So, we get to see these things with low frequency word and high cognition word in English language.  Unlike like prefixes, there are certain suffixes which also get added to words to create innovative vocabulary in English. ‘Side’: look at this, this is a suffix. It means killer. So, insecticides, pesticide, homicide, these are the words that you will hear in our regular domains in our regular uses.  So, if we understand this word, this suffix ‘side’ in these words or wherever we find them, it helps us connect, it helps us make sense of the word, make sense of the context and in terms of meaning. So they are related to killing, death. I mean forceful killing. So they become, so the meaning becomes apparent to us.  ‘Gamy ’: it is a union or marriage, so in the words like polygamy or bigamy. Actually, these are both, ‘poly’ is a prefix and ‘gamy’ is suffix. So, if you see these words, we understand what they could possibly mean.  So, ‘gen’ has literal meaning produce.  So you see carcinogen, allergen and so on.  You get more words with ‘graph ’, means writing. Words like cinematography, telegraph, geography. So, you get more and more words with these suffixes where they will just help you and give the meaning of the word. ‘Ism’, a very productive suffix, which means act of. So, words like multilingualism, journalism, feminism, socialism, so ism is a Hinduism. It is a very productive pattern for word formation. ‘Logy’ means science of or study of. You see in biology, astrology, geology. So, any word where you see ‘l o g y’, ‘logy’, it is a suffix, and it means study of. So, it will be helpful in making the word. ‘Nome’ means knowledge of. So, economy or astronomy, these are few examples where you can see the use of these words. ‘More’ means feeding, so carnivore, herbivore and so on. You will get more words.  So, in these two points that you see, we are trying to meet with some examples which is basically the point that there are some prefixes and suffixes from Greek and Latin sources, which are very productive when it comes to low frequency but high cognitive words, high cognitively loaded words in English languages, and we use them in specific domains.  Another one, that is important for, as an innovative pattern as a productive pattern of word formation in English or for that matter for the use of English is, English is one language, which is not just widely spoken across the world, widely used across the world. That it is true that English is widely spoken across the world and widely used across the world. As a result of that, it is one language which is in contact with most number of languages spoken anywhere in the world.  So, for example, it is highly unlikely for Hindi to be in contact with Spanish or let us say French or German, but English is in contact with French, German, Spanish, Italian at the same time, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bangle, Indonesian, Japanese.  It is not an overstatement i f we say English is in one way or the other, in contact with all spoken languages of the world. If that is to be given and if that is true, then we also need to understand that English will be the language which will get or borrow words from most of these sources. So, English will have words from all other languages of the world.  It is just that English spoken in India may not have high frequency words in English from Spanish or some lesser-known languages. So, that is a description of why so many words come to English and why English is such a dynamic language, and it is this dynamism in turn which makes English one of the most widely used languages of the world. I do not mean to add comments, which are not necessary for learning English, but as a footnote at this point, I do want to add that English being the most influential language across the world and English is the most widely used language of the world, not just because it was the language of British Empire — of course it was the language of the British Empire and that has a huge role to play — but another reason why English happened to be the most widely spoken language of the world is because it has accepted borrowings from most of the languages of the world, and it got itself in a position to mix and to allow mixing from other languages of the world, which is what makes English one of the most dynamic languages.  So if you look at English, it has borrowings from Celtic languages, which are neighboring languages of English, like basket, bachelor, beak, car, cross clan. title: Connecting Ideas Between and Within Sentences
text: English – II Advanced English Professor. Rajesh Kumar Department of Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Welcome to the class. Today, we are going to talk about certain terms which are helpful in making our speech or writing effective and impressive, as we understand making our speech effective through making our language effective. In the process of making our language flawless, error free, these are our goals.  We are trying to develop accuracy for the purpose of developing confidence, which comes through effective language and if making our expressions effective is the goal of communication. In order to do that, in order to do so, at this stage, I plan to introduce a few terms, few phrases, few things to you and paying attention to them takes your sentence structure, your vocabulary and expression to the next level, and you feel more comfortable. You feel more equipped to deal with formal situations of writing as well as formal and informal situations of speaking.  At the same time, you also get equipped with understanding what others mean, what others try to say and how others use these terms in their language. These terms are essentially adverbial terms. There are some phrases and some prepositional phrases and so on. As you know, prepositional phrases are all adverbial in nature, mostly adverbial in nature. So, we are going to look at some of them, and we are going to see how we use them in sentences and their larger function in a sentence is as a marker of discourse, and that is what we are saying. Connecting ideas, basically, we are talking about connecting sentences, connecting clauses and connecting ideas, which are expressed in two different sentences. How do we connect them, because connecting the two helps us build the discourse because you know, the units of languages are sound.  Then we go to words, then we go to sentences. In communication, that is in communication with others, in making a point in conversations, what becomes significant is discourse.  Creating a discourse and concluding the discourse in a convincing way is one of the salient goals of effective communication. How do we build the discourse? How we make it attractive, influential, and effective should be the goal in communication for us. We can say something, and we can make our point effectively and people should get our point, that should be the goal. To do so, that is to work around discourse, we need to know a lot more than sentences and this is where the rules of language use, particularly what to say and more importantly, what not to say becomes important.  In order to make your point in a formal situation, how to start, how to look effortless is also important. As you know, becoming effortless, that is appearing effortless in a normal communication for effectiveness, takes a lot of efforts to prepare, to work and thus to reach that point. So, these are some of the important things to keep in mind. Language wise, some of these items that we are going to discuss today are going to help us build our discourse.  And let us play around these to take a look at them and see how they work, how these elements work. So, we are basically talking about connecting ideas, that is the point here. By ideas, we mean points, that is, within a sentence or between two sentences. There are certain terms, which can be used to connect certain points within a sentence that is intro-sentential, and beyond a sentence that is between two sentences, and so on.  So, if you look at this example, ‘There was no AC in the building. As a result, the workers had to be sent home’. So, this marker, ‘as a result’, connects the two sentences that ‘there was no AC in the building’, this is one, this is one point. ‘The workers had to be sent home’, this is another point. You put them together, it still makes sense, and we can infer the connection that because there was no AC in the building, the workers had to be sent home.  But there are certain things like a phrase such as, ‘as a result of’, ‘as a result’, ‘as a result of which’, ‘as a result’. When we use these things, then this is called the discourse marker, which connects the proposition that ‘the workers had to be sent home’ with the previous one. So, ‘as a result’, makes the previous sentence a preexisting condition for doing what is being said in the second sentence. That is how we mark the discourse.  Hear me out one more time. When we say ‘as a result ’, we are connecting two sentences by making the previous one precondition, that is, what we want to say in the second sentence is predicated upon the condition expressed in the previous one. So, ‘there was no AC’ becomes the existing condition for sending workers home. So, that is the function of a phrase like this.  ‘We could go for a movie this Diwali. Alternatively, we could just stay home and enjoy sweets’. Look at this word here in italics, ‘alternatively’, it is an adverb. You this market here, it is an adverb. ‘As a result’, is also an adverb, but it is a phrase of a different type. These are two different types of phrases, but they are discourse markers.  So, in this sentence, ‘alternatively’ helps us connect and make the previous sentence, the thing expressed in the previous sentence, as an option. So, we are talking about ‘we could go for a movie this Diwali’, ‘we could stay at home and enjoy sweets’. These are the two alternatives. So, we connect it with saying ‘alternatively’, as it is obviously, these are alternatives, so we can say ‘alternatively, we could just stay home and enjoy sweets ’.  So, these are the phrases, and we can use them in our informal and formal conversations both in writing to make it connected, to make it impressive, and make it more readable. Also, the effective use, an appropriate use of these elements makes your writing readable, makes your audience not lose the point, and the same thing happens in spoken languages as well. They are like, they have greasing effect, they make things smoother.  So, look at this now. Some of these sentences, which, ‘while I was waiting, I had a cup of coffee’. So, here we are talking about two propositions again, ‘I was waiting’, ‘I had a cup of coffee’. When I say, ‘while I was waiting’, so the use of the ‘ I was waiting, I had a cup of coffee ’, it sounds very monotonous and not very engaging way of speaking or writing.  So, if we use the term, ‘while’ making the first one is the condition, ‘ while I was waiting, I had a cup of coffee ’. ‘I had a cup of coffee ’: it is also, you are also giving justification for that, justification for buying a cup of coffee for yourself. So just, it is not like I ended up buying a cup of coffee for no reason, I was just waiting. So, it was helpful in killing time, in passing time. Hence, I bought a cup of coffee.  So, this marker while’ has a lot of meaning. It tells the audience a lot more than we can assume, and in the absence of which it makes very, very crude, it is a crude presentation it is a raw presentation. However, the use o f it makes it fluid, makes it easy. ‘I will be wearing a sea blue shawl so that you can see me easily’. ‘So that’ is another phrase, which connects the two and says it is contingent upon something. So, I am going to wear blue shawl and this is contingent, this is important, because I want you to see me, identify me easily. So, that is the purpose of this phrase.  So again, at this point, take a moment and look at yourself and see whether you use these things, whether you hear when people speak these things and when you watch television, movies and listen to people, how effectively and how often people use these terms. Take an audio sample of 5 minutes from anywhere. Watch them a couple of times, mark a note of these markers and not just these markers, maybe there are more in your sample and see the purpose of why and how that speech sample is using these markers. You will get to see, the more effective the more likeable sample, speech sample a few minutes is, and that happens because that sample is more, is full of these things, is totally tossed in these elements to make it impressive. That is the purpose of doing this.  Look at it. How we use the terms like ‘and, but, or, so a semicolon or a colon’ or just a ‘hyphen’ to connect ideas between sentences and to connect two clauses in the same sentence. So, you understand we are working on connecting things. We are working on these things as not simple conjunctions, but a connector for the marking of discourse or for creating or building the discourse.  So, let us look at some of the examples. You can come up with your own examples and I sincerely suggest you hear, as I suggested the previous one, previous exercise for you to take your 5 minutes of sample from anywhere, speech sample, and it is not tough for you to do. However, I must underline it several times that to make your languages better, do this, not just as an exercise for yourself, but as a favor to yourself. You may feel you already know, you may feel you are doing that enough, but if you feel your language is still not effective, is not impressive, or you feel somewhere some urge to make your language more effective, then you do not have to wait for me to suggest you this thing.  These are the ways of examining yourself and working on your own content. So, you use your own examples with these connectors that I am talking about, and see whether they become useful, they look useful to you.  So, ‘the building was extremely well constructed and consequently difficult to demolish’. Look at this, ‘and consequently’. We are using twice, two of them. We could simply say, ‘the building was extremely well constructed, consequently, it was difficult to demolish ’, ‘and consequently difficult to demolish ’. So, after ‘and’ we are simply using this as a phrase. This is not a sentence, ‘difficult to demolish ’, meaning it was difficult to demolish. We are using these two as markers of discourse.  ‘We could fly via Singapore; ’, look at this colon. ‘...however, this is not the only way ’. To make these two sentences within one, this is the use of a semicolon here is important. After using however, we always use a comma before introducing a new clause. So, you could fly to Singapore, you could fly via Singapore, however, this is not the only way. text: English II Ms Parthia Sathyanathan Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology Chennai Hello all welcome to this module. In today's module, we will discuss degree adverbs.  So, let us start with the question, what are degree adverbs? So, degree adverbs are used before adjectives, verbs or other adverbs to give information about the extent or degree of something. For example, I am saying they are sad; then I am saying they are extremely sad. Do you think there is a difference between these two sentences? If so, then I must say that you felt that because of this word 'extremely'. That is the only difference between sentence one and sentence two.  So, the word extremely makes all the difference. This extremely actually talks about the degree of something and in this case, it is the degree of sadness there is a greater degree of sadness and therefore the word extremely is the degree adverb. Now, there are other degree adverbs as well, let us check them out.  I hate the smell of cigars. I really hate the smell of cigars. What is the degree adverb here? It is 'really' because with the word really he is, he is trying to express a greater degree of hatred that he has for the smell of cigars. She is always late. She is almost always late. What is the function of almost here? Degree adverb. So, there are quite a few degree adverbs; they are completely fair, quite, rather, slightly, too, totally, very much, very, etc. He was completely blank. It was fairly good. It was quite dark. So, you must have used these words in different sentences, and these words are degree adverbs because they give information about the extent or degree of something.  Let us check the use of very and too; these are two adverbs or degree adverbs that are often mixed up in sentences. They are often used interchangeably. It is okay to use them interchangeably in a lot of context. But if you want to improve your language and take it to a different level or now that we are looking at Advanced English grammar, let us check the accurate use of very and too in sentences.  So, before an adjective or adverb, we use 'very' to refer to a high degree and 'too' when we mean more than enough, or more than what is wanted or needed. So, 'too' has a higher degree than that of 'very'. Let us check the use of too and very, with these two examples, the weather is very hot in Chennai, it is perfect for swimming.  So, here are very is more appropriate than too, the weather was too hot in Chennai, it is perfect for swimming, it sounds okay, it is grammatically right. But the sentence would sound better if you say, or you would be more accurate if you say the weather is very hot in Chennai or the weather was very hot in Chennai, it was perfect for swimming.  Now let us check this second sentence. It is too hot to stay in this room, let us find somewhere cooler. So here, someone is saying that it is unbearably hot and therefore let us find a different room and to refer to that unbearable heat, the person has used the degree adverb too, so rather than saying very here, the use of too should be preferred.  So, I hope I made that clear. In formal spoken English particularly in negative sentences, we can sometimes use too, to mean roughly the same as very. For example, I am not too bothered about who fails, or it is also okay to say, I am not very bothered about who fails. It is not very warm today, is it? It is not very warm today. Furthermore, it is not too warm today, is it? So, both are fine, because we are using it in an informal context. But there are certain sentences where only one of these two words would fit in appropriately.  Now, let us check the use of very and very much. Can we use them interchangeably in all sentences? No, you could use very and very much interchangeably in certain contexts in certain sentences, but not in every sentence.
